> AGENT

Honest take: probably not as standalone CV entries, but worth a single line of acknowledgement.

**Why not standalone:**
- For Mercor/engineering roles, "shipped a Hugo + Decap site for a construction company" doesn't differentiate you — lots of engineers can do that. The differentiators are the AI platform work, low-latency C++, and applied ML.
- A one-page CV is brutal on space. Every line on Blueprint Builders is a line *not* on the LiteLLM/vLLM platform or Mako orderbook.
- The web work also slightly muddies the positioning — recruiters skim and pattern-match. If half your CV is web client work, they may slot you as "freelance web dev" rather than "senior systems/AI engineer."

**Why a one-liner still helps:**
- Shows you can ship end-to-end for paying customers (entrepreneurial signal).
- Justifies any gaps and demonstrates independent operation.
- Tied to a real brand (Reliq Studios) it reads as "I run a small consultancy" not "I did some side projects."

**My recommendation:** Add it as a single sub-bullet under the current "Contract" section, e.g. "Also operate Reliq Studios delivering full-stack client websites (Blueprint Builders, MassPeople, etc.)" — one line, doesn't displace the heavy material.

Based on the search results, I found information about NSE's TBT (Tick by Tick) multicast protocol, though specific peak throughput metrics aren't explicitly detailed in these search results.

The NSE MTBT Feed is the Tick By Tick data feed of NSE that disseminates information about orders and trades on a real time basis, consisting of a series of sequenced variable length messages.

TBT was disseminated on 1G network while MTBT was disseminated primarily on 10G network. TBT data compressed multiple packets into 1 LZO batch, while MTBT data had no concept of batching and was always sent uncompressed.

The search results primarily contain API specifications and protocol documentation rather than specific performance metrics like peak message rates or maximum throughput numbers. For detailed technical specifications on message rates and peak throughput, you may need to consult the official NSE MTBT API Specification documents (version 6.3 from February 2024 or later versions) directly from NSE's technical documentation portal.

I've performed a web search for information about NSE TBT NEAT protocol, UDP snapshots, TCP retransmission, decompression, and NIFTY futures/options feeds.

Here are the key findings:

## NSE Trading Protocols

NSE provides trading front-ends "NEAT" and "NEAT+" for trading. For Non-NEAT Front-end (NNF) applications, exchange-provided documents describe the protocol used for NNF applications to communicate with the Exchange's Trading System.

## Market Data Transmission

Market data is sent as broadcast based on UDP connection, with Broadcast Circuit ID (BCID) following a unidirectional path from the host end to the trading workstation, and all broadcast data are transmitted through this broadcast circuit from the host end for all traders.

## Data Decompression

NSE protocols include documentation on the decompression algorithm of broadcast data.

## NIFTY Futures and Options

TT provides access to market data for derivatives products on NSE, including the NIFTY index, which is the exchange's benchmark for the Indian equity market.

## Tick-by-Tick (TBT) Data

Tick-by-Tick Data is available exclusively for NSE stocks and F&O (Futures & Options) scrips, though it's not feasible to send each packet from the exchange to customers in real time over the internet.

The search results show that NSE maintains detailed protocol documentation for trading system connectivity, including specifications for UDP broadcast circuits, message decompression, and interactive connections for futures and options trading.

Spark Price (which owned instrument definitions) receives it.\n4. Spark Price writes the new instrument to a **file**.\n5. Based on the search results, here's what I found regarding Cisco DNA Center's rogue access point detection capabilities:

## Key Rogue Access Point Detection Features

Cisco DNA Center uses RSSI signals and triangulation from multiple APs to provide precise location information on threats on your network.

While rogue and aWIPS detection are available on individual wireless LAN controllers, using Cisco DNA Center provides multiple advantages, including providing a single point of management for multiple controllers and receiving encrypted telemetry from all controllers which it can correlate.

## Detection and Monitoring Capabilities

The Detections tab displays information such as Detecting AP, Detecting AP Site, Adhoc, Rogue SSID, RSSI (dBM), Channels, Radio Type, SNR, State, and Last Updated.

The system identifies the AP that is currently detecting the rogue AP, and if multiple APs detect the rogue, the detecting AP with the highest signal strength is displayed.

## Threat Containment

Cisco DNA Center has the ability to contain threats by either shutting down the switchport the threat is attached to, or by triggering adjacent APs to send out de-authentication frames.

Cisco DNA Center provides impact analysis so you know how many users are getting into trouble because of a given threat.

## Additional Analysis Features

Cisco DNA Center can provide a live packet capture of threats, and forensic analysis of attacks is easier when examining a PCAP file containing the raw data of the attack.

---README---
# Aether - Unified Docker Setup

Complete Docker Compose orchestration for web applications with integrated services.

## Architecture

- **sumeetsaini_com**: [Frontend](https://github.com/kungfusaini/sumeetsaini_com) web application (sumeetsaini.com)
- **vulkan**: [Backend](https://github.com/kungfusaini/vulkan) API service (vulkan.sumeetsaini.com)
- **arcanecodex**: [Hugo](https://github.com/kungfusaini/arcane-codex) static site (arcanecodex.dev)
- **gateway**: Nginx reverse proxy with SSL termination (handles all domains)
- **plausible**: Self-hosted analytics (optional in dev, enabled in production)
- **mailcow**: Email service (production only)
- **ao3**: AO3 archive reader (ashlynofourown.sumeetsaini.com)
- **reliqstudios**: Business website (reliqstudios.com)
- **reliqdigital**: Digital services site (reliq.digital)
- **bucketbot**: Automated content bucket management bot
- **goblinbot**: Telegram bot integration service

## Development

```bash
# Start development environment (without analytics)
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-dev.yml up -d

# Start with Plausible analytics (optional)
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-dev.yml -f docker-compose-plausible.yml up -d

# View logs
docker compose logs -f

# Stop services
docker compose down
```

**Access:**
- Frontend: http://localhost
- API: http://vulkan.localhost
- Arcane Codex: http://arcanecodex.localhost
- Analytics (if enabled): http://stats.localhost

**Setup for development with Plausible:**
1. Add to `/etc/hosts`: `127.0.0.1 stats.localhost`
2. Visit http://stats.localhost/register to create an account
3. Add sites: `sumeetsaini.com` and `arcanecodex.dev`
4. Note: localhost traffic is automatically filtered by Plausible

**Email:** Enabled by default with auto-generated Ethereal credentials for testing.

## Production Deployment

```bash
# Deploy all services (including Plausible analytics)
docker compose -f docker-compose.yml -f docker-compose-prod.yml -f docker-compose-mailcow.yml -f docker-compose-plausible.yml up -d
```

**Production Analytics Setup:**
1. Obtain SSL certificate: `sudo certbot certonly --standalone -d stats.sumeetsaini.com`
2. Visit https://stats.sumeetsaini.com/register to create admin account
3. Add sites: `sumeetsaini.com` and `arcanecodex.dev`
4. Analytics are automatically tracked on production domains

## SSL Management

Wildcard certificates managed via Let's Encrypt with automatic renewal.

### How SSL Renewal Works

1. **Webroot Method**: Certbot places verification files in `/var/www/letsencrypt/.well-known/acme-challenge/` on the host
2. **Nginx serves challenges**: HTTP server blocks include a location to serve these files before redirecting to HTTPS
3. **Automatic renewal**: Systemd timer runs `certbot renew` twice daily; deploy hook restarts nginx after renewal

### Adding a New Website

Follow these steps to add a new domain to the gateway:

#### 1. Obtain SSL Certificate (First!)

SSH to your VPS and get the certificate **before** creating nginx config:

```bash
# Create webroot directory if it doesn't exist (one-time setup)
sudo mkdir -p /var/www/letsencrypt/.well-known/acme-challenge

# Request SSL certificate
sudo certbot certonly --webroot --webroot-path /var/www/letsencrypt -d <domain> -d www.<domain>
```

#### 2. Create Nginx Configuration

Create `services/gateway/conf.d/prod/<domain>.conf`:

```nginx
# <domain> - Production (HTTPS)

# HTTP to HTTPS redirect with ACME challenge support
server {
    listen 80;
    listen [::]:80;  # IPv6 (required if domain has AAAA record)
    server_name <domain> www.<domain>;
```

name: Deploy to Aether

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]
  repository_dispatch:
    types: [arcanecodex-updated]

jobs:
  build-and-deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-24.04-arm
    permissions:
      contents: read
      packages: write

    steps:
    - name: Checkout code
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
      with:
        submodules: recursive
        token: ${{ secrets.VULKAN_GIT_TOKEN }}

    - name: Log in to GitHub Container Registry
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        registry: ghcr.io
        username: ${{ github.actor }}
        password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Vulkan image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: ./services/vulkan
        file: ./services/vulkan/Dockerfile.prod
        push: true
        platforms: linux/arm64
        tags: ghcr.io/kungfusaini/vulkan:latest

    - name: Build and push sumeetsaini_com image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: ./services/sumeetsaini_com
        file: ./services/sumeetsaini_com/Dockerfile.prod
        push: true
        platforms: linux/arm64
        tags: ghcr.io/kungfusaini/sumeetsaini_com:latest

    - name: Build and push gateway image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: ./services/gateway
        file: ./services/gateway/Dockerfile
        push: true
        platforms: linux/arm64
        tags: ghcr.io/kungfusaini/gateway:latest

    - name: Checkout latest arcanecodex content
      uses: actions/checkout@v4
      with:
        repository: kungfusaini/arcane-codex
        path: ./arcanecodex-latest
        token: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }}
        submodules: recursive

    - name: Build and push arcanecodex image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: ./arcanecodex-latest
        file: ./arcanecodex-latest/Dockerfile.prod
        push: true
        platforms: linux/arm64
        tags: ghcr.io/kungfusaini/arcanecodex:latest

    - name: Build and push bucketbot image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: ./services/bucketbot
        file: ./services/bucketbot/Dockerfile.prod
        push: true
        platforms: linux/arm64

name: ci

jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:

      - uses: pre-commit/action@v3.0.1

  ci:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [25.x, 24.x, 23.x, 22.x, 21.x, 20.x, 19.x, 18.x, 17.x, 16.x]
        os: [windows-latest]
        include:

            os: macos-13  # macOS on Intel
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: macos-latest  # macOS on arm64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: ubuntu-latest  # Linux on x64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: ubuntu-24.04-arm  # Linux on arm64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: windows-2025
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: windows-11-arm  # Windows on arm64
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm install
      # TODO: On Windows Node.js v11 these will fail but `make test` will succeed
      - if: matrix.node-version != '11.x'
        run: |
          npm run-script rebuild-tests
          npm test
      - run: make test

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:

env:
  CI_CHECK_FAIL: ssh2
  OPENSSL_CONF: /dev/null

jobs:
  tests-linux:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [10.16.0, 10.x, 12.x, 14.x, 16.x, 18.x, 20.x, 22.x, 24.x]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - name: Check Node.js version
        run: node -pe process.versions
      - name: Check npm version
        run: npm -v
      - name: Install Python 2.7 (node <16.x)
        if: ${{ contains(fromJSON('["10.16.0", "10.x", "12.x", "14.x"]'), matrix.node-version) }}
        uses: LizardByte/setup-python-action@v2024.1105.190605
        with:
          python-version: '2.7'
      - name: Use Python 2.7 (node <16.x)
        if: ${{ contains(fromJSON('["10.16.0", "10.x", "12.x", "14.x"]'), matrix.node-version) }}
        run: echo "PYTHON=$(which python2.7)" >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
      - name: Install module
        run: npm install
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
  tests-macos:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [16.x, 18.x, 20.x, 22.x, 24.x]
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Use Node.js ${{ matrix.node-version }}
        uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - name: Install Python 3.10
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.10'
      - name: Check Node.js version
        run: node -pe process.versions
      - name: Check npm version
        run: npm -v
      - name: Install module
        run: npm install
      - name: Run tests
        run: npm test
  tests-macos-homebrew:
    runs-on: macos-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
        with:
          persist-credentials: false
      - name: Use Node.js (latest)
        run: brew install node
      - name: Install Python 3.10
        uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with:
          python-version: '3.10'

# https://docs.github.com/en/actions/automating-builds-and-tests/building-and-testing-nodejs
# https://github.com/actions/setup-node
# https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-github-hosted-runners/using-github-hosted-runners/about-github-hosted-runners#standard-github-hosted-runners-for-public-repositories

name: ci
on:
  push:
  #  branches: [main]
  pull_request:
  #  branches: [main]
  workflow_dispatch:
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  pre-commit:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: pre-commit/action@v3.0.1

  ci:
    strategy:
      fail-fast: false
      matrix:
        node-version: [25.x, 24.x, 23.x, 22.x, 21.x, 20.x, 19.x, 18.x, 17.x, 16.x]
        os: [windows-latest]
        include:
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: macos-15-intel  # macOS on Intel
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: macos-latest  # macOS on arm64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: ubuntu-latest  # Linux on x64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: ubuntu-24.04-arm  # Linux on arm64
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: windows-2025
          - node-version: lts/*
            os: windows-11-arm  # Windows on arm64
    runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}
      - run: npm install
      # TODO: On Windows Node.js v11 these will fail but `make test` will succeed
      - if: matrix.node-version != '11.x'
        run: |
          npm run-script rebuild-tests
          npm test
      - run: make test

name: CI

on:
  push:
  pull_request:
  workflow_dispatch:

jobs:

    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    
    strategy:
      matrix:
        node-version: [14.x, 16.x, 18.x, 19.x]

      - uses: actions/checkout@v3

        uses: actions/setup-node@v3
        with:
          node-version: ${{ matrix.node-version }}

          docker --version
          node -v
          docker pull ubuntu
          pwd
          cd ../
          git clone --depth=50 --branch=master https://github.com/apocas/dockerode.git
          cd dockerode
          npm install
          cd ../docker-modem
          
      - name: NPM install
        run: npm install
      
      - name: Internal Tests
        run: npm test
            
      - name: Dockerode Tests
        run: |
          cd ../dockerode
          rm -rf ./node_modules/docker-modem
          pwd
          ls ../
          cp -R ../docker-modem ./node_modules/docker-modem
          npm test

name: clang-format Check

on: [push, pull_request]

jobs:
  # Building using the github runner environement directly.
  clang-format:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v2
    - name: Fetch origin/main
      run: git fetch origin main
    - name: List of changed file(s)
      run: git diff --name-only FETCH_HEAD

    - name: Build clang-format docker
      run: cd .github/workflows && docker build --tag=linter .
    - name: Check clang-format
      run: docker run --rm --init -v $(pwd):/repo linter:latest clang-format --version
    - name: clang-format help
      run: docker run --rm --init -v $(pwd):/repo linter:latest clang-format --help

    - name: Check current commit
      run: docker run --rm --init -v $(pwd):/repo -w /repo linter:latest sh -c "git diff --diff-filter=d --name-only FETCH_HEAD | grep '\.c$\|\.h$\|\.cc$' | xargs clang-format --style=file --dry-run --Werror "

{
  "file_path": "/Users/sumeet/matrix/web/projects/project-writeups/aether/raw.md",
  "content": "# Aether — Raw Notes for CV\n\n> Personal Docker-based infrastructure hosting all of Sumeet's web services. Public on GitHub (`kungfusaini/aether`). Running in prod since ~September 2025.\n\n---\n\n## Sumeet's dictation (verbatim, lightly cleaned)\n\n### Why it exists\n- \"I wanted to host my own stuff and have my own place to play around with.\"\n- Built **entirely for learning** — wanted to do everything himself.\n\n### What it runs (all in prod, since ~Sept 2025)\n- **sumeetsaini.com** — personal portfolio frontend.\n- **Vulkan** — personal backend API (`vulkan.sumeetsaini.com`).\n- **Arcane Codex** — Hugo static blog.\n- **Nginx gateway** — reverse proxy + SSL termination across all domains.\n- **Plausible Analytics** — self-hosted.\n- **Mailcow** — self-hosted email.\n- **Reliq Studios, Reliq Digital, Reliq Labs** — three business sites.\n- **Bucketbot, Goblinbot** — Telegram bots.\n- ~~AO3 reader~~ — personal gift project for his girlfriend; not relevant.\n\n### The learning → professional pipeline (the strongest framing for CV)\n> \"It taught me about Docker, it taught me about CI/CD, and I was able to **implement the stuff that I'm working on at Elijah right now because of this training**.\"\n\n→ **Aether is where Sumeet learned the Docker + CI/CD discipline he then applied to the stealth AI startup's production platform.** That's the CV-worthy framing: not \"I built a personal homelab,\" but \"I built personal infra deliberately to learn skills I now apply professionally.\"\n\n---\n\n## What the repo actually does (evidence pulled from `kungfusaini/aether`)\n\n### Architecture\n- **Docker Compose orchestration** of 10+ production services.\n- Multiple compose files for env separation: `docker-compose.yml` (base), `docker-compose-dev.yml`, `docker-compose-prod.yml`, `docker-compose-plausible.yml`, `docker-compose-mailcow.yml`. Layered compose-overlay pattern.\n- **Nginx gateway** with SSL termination, wildcard cert support, IPv4+IPv6.\n\n### CI/CD (`.github/workflows/deploy.yml`)\n- Triggers on push to `main` **and** on **cross-repo `repository_dispatch`** from `kungfusaini/arcane-codex` (so the blog repo can trigger an aether rebuild when content updates).\n- Builds images for **linux/arm64** — VPS is ARM-based # Argus

Personal AI agent system running on a Hetzner VPS. Telegram is the primary interface.

## Architecture

Two-tier agent: a fast chat model handles conversation and routes tasks to a worker model that has tools and domain context.

```
argus/                    — Argus agent (code + ICM context)
├── src/                  — Core Python modules
├── domains/              — Domain contracts and chat prompts
├── references/           — Stable reference docs
├── fitness_web/          — Fitness dashboard (Flask + Mapbox + Chart.js)
└── CLAUDE.md             — Worker spec + domain routing (ICM Layer 0)

infra/                    — Docker services
├── litellm/              — LiteLLM proxy + Postgres
├── flatnotes/            — Shared notes app
├── vikunja/              — Task management
└── nanoproxy/            — NanoProxy for open-source model tool calling

services/                 — Systemd unit files
nginx/                    — Nginx configs (deployed via stow)
deploy.sh                 — Deploy nginx + systemd services
```

## Key Concepts

- **ICM (Intelligent Context Management):** Layered prompt system — Layer 0 (CLAUDE.md: worker spec + routing) → Layer 1 (domain contracts) → Layer 2 (references)
- **NanoProxy:** Bridges unreliable tool calling for open-source models
- **Obsidian Vault:** Knowledge graph at `/root/codex/` — wiki, journal, personal notes
- **Vikunja:** Task management via MCP (projects: Inbox, Argus, Personal, Research, Project Pyari)

## Services

| Service | Type | URL |
|---------|------|-----|
| Argus | systemd | Telegram: @argus_custom_ai_bot |
| Journal Bot | systemd | Telegram (separate bot) |
| Fitness Dashboard | systemd | https://fit.argbox.net |
| OpenCode | systemd | https://code.argbox.net |
| LiteLLM | Docker | https://llm.argbox.net |
| Vikunja | Docker | https://task.argbox.net |
| Flatnotes | Docker | https://notes.argbox.net |
| NanoProxy | Docker | localhost:8787 (internal) |

## Recovery from scratch

### 1. Clone and set up secrets
```bash
git clone git@github.com:kungfusaini/argus-agents.git /root/argus-agents
cd /root/argus-agents

# Create .env files (not in git)
# argus/.env            — TELEGRAM_BOT_TOKEN, JOURNAL_BOT_TOKEN, LLM keys, etc.
# infra/litellm/.env    — DATABASE_URL, UI_USERNAME, UI_PASSWORD, API keys
# infra/flatnotes/.env  — FLATNOTES_USERNAME, FLATNOTES_PASSWORD, FLATNOTES_SECRET_KEY
```

### 2. Python environment
```bash
cd argus
python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate
pip install -r requirements.txt
```

### 3. Deploy nginx + systemd services
```bash
cd /root/argus-agents
bash deploy.sh
```

### 4. Start Docker services
```bash
cd infra/litellm && docker compose up -d
cd ../flatnotes && docker compose up -d
cd ../vikunja && docker compose up -d
cd ../nanoproxy && docker compose up -d
```

### 5. Start systemd services
```bash
systemctl enable --now argus fitness_web journal_bot opencode
```

### 6. Install OpenCode
```bash
curl -fsSL https://opencode.ai/install | bash
# Create /root/.opencode/.env with OPENCODE_SERVER_USERNAME and OPENCODE_SERVER_PASSWORD
systemctl restart opencode
```

### 7. Restore flatnotes data
```bash
cd infra/flatnotes/data
git clone git@github.com:kungfusaini/flatnotes-backup.git .
```

### 8. Set up cron
```bash
crontab -e
# Add: */15 * * * * /root/argus-agents/flatnotes/backup.sh
```
```

# Argus Worker

You are the worker agent in a two-tier system. A fast chat model handles user conversation on Telegram and dispatches tasks to you. You receive a task description and intent, do the work using your tools, and return a clear result summary.

You do NOT chat with the user directly — the chat model handles that. Focus on executing the task accurately and narrating your progress.

## Routing

### Domains
| Domain | Path | When to load |
|--------|------|-------------|
| chat | domains/chat/CONTEXT.md | Always — read this on every message |
| tasks | domains/tasks/CONTEXT.md | Creating, listing, updating, or discussing tasks |
| system | domains/system/CONTEXT.md | Questions about architecture, VPS, services, or how you work |
| validation | domains/validation/CONTEXT.md | Health checks, system validation, debugging |
| knowledge | domains/knowledge/CONTEXT.md | Daily roundup, vault entity management, cross-linking |
| fitness | domains/fitness/CONTEXT.md | Workout generation, exercise programming, measurements |
| recipes | domains/recipes/CONTEXT.md | Saving, browsing, or searching recipes |
| notes | domains/notes/CONTEXT.md | Reading, writing, or searching shared notes |

### References
| File | Contents |
|------|----------|
| references/architecture.md | Full system architecture, VPS services, stack, design philosophy |
| references/telegram.md | Telegram bot commands, constraints, how to add new commands |

### Important
When making changes that affect Telegram commands, update `references/telegram.md` to keep it in sync.

Read the relevant domain contract with `read_file` before acting. Don't assume rules — check the contract first.

---DESIGN SPEC head---
\chapter{Design \& Specification}
\begin{itemize}
\item The model should contain two heads
\begin{itemize}
\item One head will be tasked with predicting the image class

\item One head will be tasked with predicting information about the pertubation
\end{itemize}
\item Gaussian noise examples with be generated with a simple additive gaussian noise for adversarial training
\begin{itemize}
\item A portion of training data will be taken

\item Random gaussian noise will be generated using Numpy’s normal function
\item A label will be preserved indicating the standard deviation of the noise
\item The noise will be added to the original image
\item The network will be trained to identify the original class label and the standard deviation
\end{itemize}
\item Style Transfer examples with be generated with a neural network
\begin{itemize}
\item A portion of training data will be taken

\item A random texture from a limited pool with be applied to the image using the style transfer network

\item A label will be preserved indicating the texture that has been applied

\item The network will be trained to identify the original class label and the applied texture
\end{itemize}
\item Foolbox\cite{Rauber2018} will be used to verify the effectiveness of the model using its benchmarking capabilities
\end{itemize}

Chapter 1


Introduction

Throughout the group project this year I had an amazing opportunity to work on a real-world

problem provided to us by Bristol Airport. I was lucky to have a great team, one in which each

member pulled their weight and contributed equally to the project. That is not to say that the

project was always smooth. Due to the team having to majorly pivot the project 3 times, it

was difficult to know what to do next. Going into the project, I wanted to develop my skills

chiefly in developing artificial intelligence. Initially, it seemed that the project would allow for

this, but in the end, the skills I developed were much different than what I anticipated.

   Along with developing skills with python, AWS technologies and REST APIs, I also im-

proved other non-technical skills, such as communicating with stakeholders, understanding

client needs, and bringing out the best in my team. My proudest technical accomplishment

was the data extraction and management that I performed. It was a difficult problem for me

to solve, but without it, the team would not have been able to produce the data visualisation

tool to the same quality as we did, if at all. My proudest accomplishment overall was the final

demo day. I worked very hard to prepare a script for the demo which was the culmination of

all our hard work. I was extremely happy with the way I presented our tool to the public and

how I handled tricky questions, which required knowing the project and stakeholders in detail.

The script I wrote for the demo allowed everyone to express the value of the tool and underline

their contributions during the presentations.

   This report will outline my technical contributions to the project, as well as detail the key

skills I utilised and obtained during the project. I will conclude by reflecting on my work over

the year and discuss how I will continue to develop the valuable skills I’ve learnt.




                                                 2
Chapter 2


Technical Contributions

In the early stages of the project, our team was divided into 3 sections. These were the front-

end team, the AI team and the data analysis, which I was the sole member of. When the team

got started with the bulk of the project, we divided it into two teams. Two members worked

on the front end, while the other two worked on the back end. I was not part of either of these.

Instead, I worked as a float on the project, contributing to any task that needed extra hands.

Instead of listing these smaller contributions, below I will discuss my three major contributions

to the project.



2.1     Building the Dataset

When we first gained access to the data, I was in charge of understanding it and deciding

how it could be useful to our team while the others worked on the AI tool and the simulation

visualisation, which was eventually abandoned. When experimenting with the API that Bristol

Airport had given us, I discovered that it was slow, and often ran into bugs. Due to this, I

decided to build a tool to extract all the data from the API so that we had our own local copy,

freely accessible. This ended up becoming the backbone of the project. If we continued to use

the API, the entire team would need to know how to use it, and we would have to mitigate

the errors. Also, our tool would be built around extracting data from an API, which does not

accurately model how the airport would integrate the tool. By creating our own local copy, the

team could focus directly on the data. But doing this required me to learn a few new techniques

and technologies.

   I had very little experience with REST APIs. I was only familiar with them in a general



                                               3
context but had never developed any tool to interact with them. I had to learn how to use the

’requests’ module of python and understand how to correctly format an API call to send the

request, but also how to receive it. I also had to become familiar with the ’pandas’ library of

python. This library allowed me to keep the data formatted in a data frame, which keeps it

organised and in an easily readable format. The most difficult part about this tool was making

it robust. It took around 30 minutes to grab the data from just one of the 3 sources. If the

API ran into errors, the whole program would stop and all progress would be lost. I came

to understand that the API would fail during certain months, so I had to adapt the tool to

accommodate this.

   Once the tool worked correctly, I built a CSV file for each of the 3 datasets. Now the

team had access to the data without reliance on the API. This success was a milestone that

indicated to me I had made measurable progress in working with REST APIs and also pandas.

An example of the code is shown in figure 2.1.



2.2        Data Analysis

Now I had access to data, I attempted to perform some data analysis. This required taking

two steps. The first was non-technical (understanding the data and what it represents), and

the second was learning how to manipulate the data and display it. I performed a multitude of

experiments using a Juypter notebook but lacked the technical knowledge to format the data

correctly. I would constantly run into type errors, arithmetic errors and table formatting errors

because I did not understand how to work with the data. For example, when working to try and

calculate the distribution of stay durations in the car park, I needed to perform mathematical

operations on timestamped data, dividing each timestamp into smaller bins. I had to learn how

to use more complex pandas functions, like ’TimeDelta’ to achieve this goal. My pandas skills

increased, but I also had to learn how to use ’Matplotlib’. I had very limited experience with the

library beforehand, so I watched tutorials and delved into the documentation to understand how

I could visualise the insights I had gathered. Figure 2.2 shows two examples of visualisations I

created.

   Even though the exact code I wrote for these visualisations was not used in the final project,

this technical work proved useful in other ways. When the team had to pivot away from AI, we

had a working prototype for data visualisation. This gave us confidence that this new direction

of the project would be feasible, and the technical grounding had been laid. I now also had a

great understanding of the data, how to manipulate it, and what insights could be gained. I


                                                 4
Figure 2.1: A snippet of code showing the headers, format for an API call, and the command
line utility I built to easily interact with the tool.




                                            5
                                     Figure 2.2: Caption


was able to pass this knowledge on to my team, which greatly sped up the process of developing

our solution. Due to this, I was able to pass to my team a list of metrics, along with how to

calculate them, which lead to an increase in the number of metrics we were able to implement.

   The successful production of these graphs was another milestone that indicated my skills

had improved. When pitching our new project direction to the sponsor, he was intrigued by

the graphs I created and gave us his approval. Without this, we might not have taken this path

in the project, which was ultimately very successful.



2.3     Populating the Database

Local CSVs are a problem as the team cannot easily interact with them unless they have a

copy. Also, it would be unwise to build our solution around CSVs as Bristol Airport does not

store its data in this way. We decided we should populate a DynamoDB hosted on AWS. This

ended up being difficult and time-consuming for me.

   Firstly, I had to create a new database in the cloud. Then, I learnt how to use the ’Boto3’

library for python, which allows the user to interact with AWS services through code. Once this

was set up, I attempted to use the library’s ’batch write’ function to connect to the database

and write each entry of the CSV into it, with the appropriate datatype and headers. After

ironing out formatting and data type bugs, the code was successfully populating the database.

However, this was a slow process, taking over 24 hours just to populate one of the tables, even

when turning off write limits for the database.

   I needed to find another way to populate the database. Through research, I learned about

S3 buckets and discovered that if the data was already in the cloud, it would be much quicker

to populate the database. I set up an S3 bucket using the AWS dashboard, and once again


                                                  6
Figure 2.3: Code showing the lambda functions used to populate the booking data into the
database


used the ’Boto3’ library, this time to place the CSVs into the bucket. Following this, I built

a workflow using AWS lambda to populate each of the 3 tables, one for each CSV file. The

lambda workflow involved 3 separate functions. One to get the data from the S3 bucket, one

to populate the database, and a third to coordinate these actions. With everything up and

running, I managed to populate all the data in around 30 minutes, a huge improvement. This

effort was vital in bringing the team’s data into the cloud.

Solo developer on the ground, senior dev oversight, ~few months end-to-end.\n\n---\n\n## Sumeet's dictation\n\n### Scope & coverage\n- Targeted **NIFTY 50 futures & options**, possibly **NIFTY 100 futures & options** (uncertain).\n- \"Previously untapped market\" framing: Mako wasn't trading India at all before this. The handler built the *pricing-side* foundation — feeding data into Mako's data pipeline (Kafka), capturing live, replaying historic PCAPs, giving strategy teams something to build on.\n- They weren't live-trading NSE through this — it was the foundation to *be able to* trade.\n\n### Architecture\n- Built within Mako's internal **Spark** framework:\n  - **Spark Price**: pricing, orderbooks, instrument definitions historically lived here.\n  - **Spark Order**: order routing (depended on Spark Price for instrument definitions).\n- For the NSE work he was \"just doing the pricing side\" — Spark Price + Spark Order on the NSE side.\n- Generic market processor base class in C++20 (template-based); exchange-specific implementation on top.\n\n### C++ / infra\n- **C++20**, heavily template-based.\n- **Solarflare NICs** (kernel bypass). Kernel-bypass + Linux specifics abstracted away by internal libraries; Sumeet doesn't claim deep ownership there.\n- **IPC**: pushed processed market data out to downstream consumers via an internal IPC queue mechanism. \"It's a famous protocol/library, I can't remember the name.\" → unresolved.\n- Lots of internal libraries handling things like **feed arbitrage** (A-feed vs B-feed) etc. — he didn't reimplement those.\n\n### Orderbook\n- \"Kind of built it from scratch, kind of not.\" Existing orderbook implementations for other exchanges; adapted/built the NSE-specific one on top of the shared base.\n\n### Protocol specifics (NSE MTBT)\n- **MTBT** = Multicast Tick-By-Tick. NSE's F&O market data feed.\n- Per NSE docs: MTBT is 10G, uncompressed; TBT (older feed) was 1G, LZO-batched. The decompression Sumeet had to implement was on the TBT-style feed → NSE TBT uses **LZO**.\n- Two feed types handled:\n  - MTBT (tick-by-tick): order/trade tick stream.\n  - NF/stats feed: opens, closes, statistics.\n- **Gap recovery**:\n  - **TCP gap fill** for smaller gaps.\n  - **UDP snapshot** for periodic snapshots + larger recovery.\n- Protocol had quirks; documentation is in the public NSE archive (refs below).\n\n### Latency\n- Sumeet didn't own latency measurement; doesn't have a number.\n- Boss had a quoted \"magic figure\" — either **100 microseconds** or **100 nanoseconds** wire-to-wire round-trip target. Sumeet uncertain which.\n- Concrete reliability fact: the handler **kept up live without falling behind** during the busiest periods.\n\n### Testing & deployment\n- UAT testing.\n- Replay against captured PCAPs (development and regression).\n- Live capture for verification.\n- Took it from \"one PCAP + protocol documentation\" to working market processor in prod within a few months.\n\n### Stakeholder coordination\nSolo developer ownership, coordinating across:\n- The broker (PCAPs, connectivity).\n- The exchange directly (protocol queries, certification).\n- Mako's data pipeline team (Kafka / cloud ingest).\n- Mako's infrastructure team (sizing, throughput requirements, getting his own box).\n- Senior stakeholders globally for progress reporting.\n- Advised internal teams on capacity sizing and machine requirements.\n\n### The legacy handler rewrite\n- **Interactive Data (IDC)** is a market data aggregator.\n- Old market processor for the Interactive Data feed existed; rewrote it into Mako's **Spark FI** framework.\n- Result: faster, more reliably fed Mako's data pipeline, standardised with the rest of the Spark codebase.\n\n### The combo / multi-leg latency win\n\n**Before:**\n1. Strategy via Spark Order creates a combo instrument → sends to exchange.\n2. Exchange returns instrument definition.\n3. Spark Price (owner of instrument definitions) receives it.\n4. Spark Price writes the new instrument to a **file**.\n5. Spark Order polls that file until the new instrument shows up.\n6. Then Spark Order routes on it.\n\nTotal lag: **~2 seconds**.\n\n**After (Sumeet's fix — built `Spark Info`):**\n- New component, **Spark Info**, owns instrument-definition flow.\n- Spark Order requests creation → exchange → Spark Info receives → fans out instrument definition **in parallel** to both Spark Price and Spark Order via proper IPC queues (not file-based).\n- Removed the ~2s lag for multi-leg order submission.\n\n### IPC queue work\n- Replaced file-based / large-blob exchange of instrument definitions with proper IPC queues.\n- Prevented queue flooding so price information (latency-critical) wasn't starved by instrument-definition traffic.\n\n---\n\n## Open / unresolved facts\n\n- TBT vs MTBT — exactly which feed(s) the Mako NSE handler consumed. Worth resolving precisely.\n- The \"famous IPC library\" name — likely Aeron, possibly proprietary; Sumeet can't recall.\n- The \"100us vs 100ns\" boss-quoted target — uncertain which.\n- Confirmation the handler ran in production at Mako before Sumeet left → yes, deployed into prod, capturing live data for the data pipeline; not yet trading.\n- NIFTY 50 vs NIFTY 100 — uncertain.\n\n---\n\n## Public NSE protocol references\n\n- NSE MTBT API Specification v6.3 (Feb 2024): https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/web/sites/default/files/inline-files/Realtime_CM_CD_TBT%20ver%206.3.pdf\n- NSE MTBT API Specification v6.2 (Sept 2021): https://archives.nseindia.com/content/press/Realtime_CM_CD_TBT.pdf\n- \"TBT vs MTBT data dissemination\" (Sanchety, Medium): https://medium.com/@sanchety.deepak/data-dissemination-part-2-tbt-vs-mtbt-data-dissemination-969606c7d6e7\n- NNF (Non-NEAT Front-end) protocol: https://nsearchives.nseindia.com/web/sites/default/files/inline-files/TP_FO_Trimmed_NNF_PROTOCOL_9.38_0.pdf\n\nPer Sanchety: TBT was 1G, LZO-batched; MTBT is 10G, uncompressed.\n"

Based on the search results, here's what I found about the Google X-Y-Z resume formula and hiring manager advice:

## The Formula

The X-Y-Z formula is: Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y] by doing [Z]. This formula was outlined by Laszlo Bock, a former Google Senior Vice President of People Operations.

## How Each Component Works

- **[X] - Achievement**: Always start with an action verb, add a metric, and explain how you achieved it.
- **[Y] - Measurement**: The quantifiable metric or result
- **[Z] - Method**: Describe the action taken to achieve the result.

## Why It Works

The XYZ method resume approach works because it helps recruiters quickly ascertain: what did you improve, by how much, and how? Instead of listing your job responsibilities, the XYZ method helps you take a results-first approach that shows your accomplishments with key metrics.

## Practical Example

Instead of saying you "increased sales," use the XYZ structure: Increased sales (X) by 25% (Y) by launching a new line of business in Q1 (Z).

## Hiring Manager Perspective

Recruiters and hiring managers often skim resumes due to time constraints. The XYZ Method organizes information concisely, ensuring your key accomplishments are highlighted.

Here are the key resume tips for FAANG senior and staff engineers from hiring managers in 2025:

## Length and Format
A second page is defensible for senior or staff engineers with a long track record, but only if the extra material is strong. Use a single-column layout so dates, titles, and technologies are easy to parse.

## Scannability is Critical
As a hiring manager at a FAANG company, they spend less than ten seconds on the first pass and are searching for the tech stack first, then quantified impact, moving on if both cannot be found in the top half of the first page. The Skills section belongs at the very top of your resume, directly below your contact information, since the hiring manager needs to validate your tech stack before they will invest time in reading about your experience.

## For Staff-Level Positions
Recruiters are searching for scope, architecture ownership, and cross-team impact—proof you influence ambiguous problems beyond your immediate team's boundaries. Balance scope with quantified results, such as "Defined and rolled out global multi-tier cache across 12 services, cutting p95 latency from 280ms to 190ms and lifting quarterly conversion 4%".

The strongest resumes show independent decision-making, high-trust ownership, and work that influenced architecture or business outcomes without heavy supervision.

## Impact Over Tasks
Resumes competent for FAANG tend to place the impact before the description of responsibilities, using the STAR method (Situation, Task, Action, Result). FAANG recruiters look for evidence of impact, scalability, and leadership potential, valuing resumes that highlight measurable results, cross-functional collaboration, and problem-solving at scale.

## Tailoring Your Resume
Keep your core resume the same, but adjust the order of bullet points and emphasize achievements that align with each company's known preferences.

## Resume Best Practices for AI/ML Engineers in 2026

### Key Skills & Specializations
NLP/LLM and MLOps tracks currently have the highest hiring demand and salary premiums in 2025–2026. State your specialization: NLP, LLMs, CV, or MLOps, add one meaningful metric (latency reduction, accuracy boost, cost savings), and mention a technical focus area relevant to the role you want.

### Project Portfolio
Avoid building Titanic survival predictor, MNIST classifier, or Iris dataset classifier as they will not impress hiring managers; instead build things that show production thinking — deployment, monitoring, real business framing. Projects should require tools expected in real jobs — Docker, MLflow, Airflow, HuggingFace, FastAPI, and Kubernetes.

### Resume Structure & ATS Optimization
ATS and humans both use the skills section to check if your toolkit matches the job requirements; only list tools you can defend in an interview and prioritize the skills the job description repeats. If the JD mentions "PyTorch" and "MLflow" repeatedly, make sure those show up in relevant places.

### Frontier Labs Specific
Every frontier lab has tribal knowledge that takes years to absorb — the memory math, the failure modes, the things senior engineers just know, and it's also what they test for in interviews. Frontier lab (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind): total comp regularly exceeds $500K at senior level.

### Cloud & Certifications
Most employers might expect you to be able to use tools like AWS or Microsoft Azure, so if you are familiar with cloud technology, indicate it in your resume.

Based on the search results, here's what Jane Street looks for in resumes for software engineers and quant traders:

## Resume Structure & Key Sections

Jane Street values a "Math" section listing relevant coursework (Real Analysis, Combinatorics, Stochastic Processes), and if you have a high GPA (3.8+), display it prominently.

Competitions are the highest-value section—"USAMO Qualifier," "Putnam Top 500," or "Codeforces Candidate Master" should be at the top.

For projects, describe the technical difficulty—"Implemented a compiler in OCaml" is better than "Built a React Native To-Do app."

## What They Value

Jane Street looks for quantitative pedigree (degrees in math, statistics, physics, CS, or engineering from target schools), and internship history at firms like Two Sigma, Citadel, D.E. Shaw, Jump, HRT, or FAANG software engineering.

Tip: Lead with quantitative coursework and competitions before work experience, include mental math or trading game competitions, and be explicit about programming languages, especially Python and OCaml.

## Cover Letters & Application Process

Jane Street explicitly states that cover letters are not required and are rarely read. Unless you have a specific anomaly to explain (e.g., a 3-year gap year or a radical career switch), do not submit one.

Unlike some firms that rely on automated screening, Jane Street reviews every application with a human—which means your resume gets read. A well-crafted resume with strong quantitative credentials has a real shot regardless of which university you attended.

## No Prior Finance Experience Required

You don't need to know OCaml or have experience within finance—Jane Street will teach you everything you need to know.

Jane Street is looking for sharp, curious minds who enjoy solving problems. If you come from a maths, physics, computer science, or engineering background, you're likely more competitive than someone with a finance degree.

I've completed the web search for that query. Here's a summary of the key insights from the results:

## Key Findings on Staff/Principal Engineer Resume Framing

**Scope and Ownership:**

For a Staff Software Engineer, resumes should combine years of experience with clear markers of technical ownership, delivery impact, and team influence. A Staff Engineer is a deeply technical individual contributor whose impact extends beyond their immediate team, often touching several teams or an entire product area.

A Staff Engineer's scope is their team's domain plus the adjacent systems that interact with it. In contrast, a Principal Engineer's scope is an entire product area or organization, owning the technical direction of how dozens of services fit together into a coherent architecture.

**Cross-Team Impact:**

Staff Engineers propose, champion, and implement technical initiatives that improve performance, reliability, or developer velocity for dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers. The fundamental difference between Senior and Staff isn't technical skill—it's operating scope. A Senior Engineer excels within their team. A Staff Engineer excels across teams, navigating organizational complexity to solve problems no single team can address.

**Resume Framing:**

Senior engineer resumes should show system ownership, cross-team influence, trade-off decisions, prioritization, and measurable outcomes. Each bullet should show what you owned, what changed, and how broad the impact was. Good examples include improving uptime, reducing processing time, strengthening release quality, mentoring engineers, or shaping product delivery with product managers.

Based on the search results, here are the common mistakes and hiring manager pet peeves for software engineer resumes, especially at the senior level:

## Top Resume Mistakes for Senior-Level Engineers

**1. Lack of Impact and Quantifiable Results**

The most common mistake is when resumes read like a boring list of chores. Every piece of code you've written should have a quantifiable impact attached to it. Rather than simply stating responsibilities, frame your work around the results you delivered using the formula: "Achieved [X] by doing [Y], which resulted in [Z]."

**2. Spelling, Grammar, and Formatting Errors**

A misspelled word is a glaring red flag, and after the first or second error, many hiring managers will stop reading the resume altogether. Resume formatting errors are major hiring manager pet peeves that instantly hurt your chances, with clean, consistent design being one of the most important resume best practices.

**3. Generic and Non-Tailored Resumes**

Every job posting has keywords representing the employer's pain points, but many applicants make the mistake of having one resume for all job postings, which causes them to miss out on what the employer is looking for.

**4. Missing Contact Information**

Nearly 70% of recruiters said resume deal-breakers like missing contact information or an unprofessional email address could cause them to immediately dismiss a candidate from the hiring process.

**5. Disjointed Career Progression**

Recruiters want to see progression: junior → mid → senior → lead, and a scattered list of jobs without context looks unfocused.

**6. Lack of Soft Skills and Leadership Examples**

Technical prowess alone isn't enough, as teams need collaboration, communication, and problem-solving abilities.

**7. Poor Technical Skill Presentation**

Avoid simply naming tools or using a generic skills section without providing context or tying it to a specific experience, as this misses the opportunity to show applied skills that weaken the resume's impact.

## Web Search Results: Resume Bullet Points, STAR Method, Quantified Impact, and Action Verbs

Here's a comprehensive overview of best practices for crafting resume bullet points using the STAR method with quantified impact and strong action verbs:

### The STAR Method Framework

The STAR method refers to Situation, Task, Action, and Result, a framework that helps job seekers structure resume bullet points to showcase experiences and achievements effectively. To write STAR achievements, describe the situation you faced, the task you were assigned, the actions you took, and the results you achieved—allowing you to present your accomplishments effectively.

### Action Verbs: The Foundation

Start your bullet points with strong action verbs. Strong action verbs include "led," "developed," "implemented," "optimized," "reduced," "increased," "managed," "generated," "negotiated," and "launched," while you should avoid passive verbs like "responsible for" or "assisted with." Starting with action verbs is important as these verbs demonstrate ownership over your work and stand out to recruiters.

### Quantifying Impact: The Critical Element

Quantify your work and achievements where possible. Begin with strong action verbs, incorporate relevant keywords, and always end with quantifiable results—resumes with quantified achievements are 40% more likely to get interviews. Numbers make your accomplishments more concrete; whenever possible, include measurable results such as percentages, dollar amounts, or time saved to add weight to your achievements.

### Bullet Point Formula

An impact-focused bullet point follows a simple formula: [Action Verb] + [Task/Responsibility] + [Quantifiable Result] + (Optional: Context/Tools). For example: "Optimized the company's supply-chain workflow, reducing lead time by 23% using Lean Six Sigma methods."

### Senior IC (Individual Contributor) Considerations

Choose an action verb that describes what YOU did and what YOUR contribution was (NOT your TEAM!) to the project/activity. This is particularly important for senior-level individual contributors who need to demonstrate personal leadership and impact without necessarily managing a team.

### Practical Examples

You might explain how you developed a new sales strategy that increased sales by 40% and exceeded quarterly targets by 15%. Instead of writing "Responsible for customer service," a STAR-formatted bullet might read: "Resolved escalated customer complaints during peak holiday season by implementing a new ticket prioritization system, reducing response time by 40% and improving satisfaction ratings from 3.2 to 4.7/5."

OK — here's the dump. Synthesised from Google's hiring research, FAANG hiring managers, frontier-lab insiders, eye-tracking studies, Jane Street's actual public guidance, and a few thousand reviewed resumes' worth of pattern across the industry.

---

# The state-of-the-art on tech CVs

## 1. The reading reality — what's actually happening

Hiring managers spend **~7.4 seconds** on the first pass. Eye-tracking studies show:

- They read in an **F-pattern**: top line, then down the left margin, partial reads across.
- **Six fixation points capture ~80% of attention**: name, current title, current company, dates of recent roles, education, top-of-page bullets.
- **Dates, company names, and job titles get 67% more visual attention** than the bullets themselves.
- The yes/no decision is often made **before a single bullet has been read** — based on pattern-recognition signals: formatting quality, information density, visual hierarchy.
- For tech roles specifically, **GitHub links and certifications in the header get 60% more attention** than in other industries.
- **The first bullet of each role is read 3.5× more often than the fourth.**

**Implication:** the top third of page 1 is the entire CV in practice. Everything below is a tiebreaker. Your strongest, most quantified, most senior-signalling bullet should be the **first bullet of your current role.**

---

## 2. The Google X-Y-Z formula (Laszlo Bock, ex-SVP People Ops)

The single most-cited bullet structure in modern tech CV advice:

> **"Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y] by doing [Z]"**

- **X** = the achievement (with an action verb)
- **Y** = the quantified result
- **Z** = the method / what you did

Concrete example:
- Bad: *"Worked on the search infrastructure."*
- Better: *"Improved search."*
- X-Y-Z: *"Improved search relevance (X) by 18% on the long-tail query distribution (Y) by replacing the BM25 ranker with a learned cross-encoder (Z)."*

The formula forces the writer to lead with **what changed** rather than **what they touched**.

## 3. STAR vs X-Y-Z — when to use which

**STAR** (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is older, more verbose, better for interviews and behavioural questions. On a CV bullet, STAR is usually too long.

**X-Y-Z is the CV version of STAR.** Same content, denser packaging. Most senior engineers don't have a "Situation/Task" worth spelling out — the role title does that. Skip to X-Y-Z.

---

## 4. Quantifying when you have no clean number

This is where most senior-eng CVs fail: the work is real but the metrics never existed. Hiring managers know this. **Substitute outcome signals when you can't get a number:**

- **Counterfactual** — "what would have been broken / impossible without it." *"Built X — without which the Y release would have been blocked."*
- **Selection / endorsement** — *"Selected by [stakeholder] for [thing]"*, *"Recognised by [PMs] as [thing]"*. Borrows credibility from the stakeholder.
- **First-of / before-after** — *"IBM's first working rogue-AP detection across the Hursley estate."* The "first working" is the result.
- **Audience scale** — *"used by N services / N engineers / the platform team."*
- **Authority granted** — *"granted code-quality authority across the repo, authoring the 515-line standards the team enforces."*
- **Permission unlocked** — *"unblocked the firm's first ingest from the Indian market."* Not a number, but a clear before/after.

The trap to avoid: "**enabled the team to ...**" without saying what the team then did. Always close the loop.

---

## 5. Verb hygiene — what to kill

Hiring managers report instant pattern-skip on these:

- **"Responsible for ..."** — passive, scope-only, no result.
- **"Helped with ..."**, **"Assisted ..."** — diminishes ownership.
- **"Worked on ..."** — meaningless. Everyone worked on something.
- **"Utilized ..."** — pretentious "used". Use "used".
- **"Various ..."** — vagueness. Pick the specific ones.
- **"Successfully ..."** — implied. If you mention it, it succeeded.
- **"Spearheaded ..."** — overused; reads as buzzword to anyone over 30.

**Action verbs that age well:** Led, Built, Designed, Shipped, Migrated, Rewrote, Cut, Reduced, Eliminated, Owned, Drove, Established, Authored, Re-architected.

For senior/staff: **Owned, Drove, Established, Authored, Re-architected** signal scope; **Built, Shipped, Cut** signal delivery.

---

## 6. Senior vs Staff vs Principal — the scope signals on the page

A subtle but important distinction the eye-tracking and hiring-manager studies surface:

- **Senior**: ownership *within a team's domain.* Bullets describe components shipped, features owned, individual systems built.
- **Staff**: ownership *across teams.* Bullets describe initiatives that unblocked multiple teams, standards that propagated, architectures that defined how N services interact.
- **Principal**: ownership *of an entire product area or organisation.* Bullets describe the technical direction the org now takes, the trade-offs made at scale, the people coached into staff roles.

If you're applying for staff, the CV needs evidence that **your work touched things outside your immediate team's boundary**. Concretely: cross-team migrations, standards authored, platforms used by others, architecture decisions adopted org-wide.

Most "stuck at senior" engineers have **excellent senior bullets** but no bullets that *prove they operated above their team*. That's the gap to look for.

---

## 7. Frontier-lab and AI-specific resume tips

From Vlad Feinberg (ex-Google researcher) and the latest hiring guidance for OpenAI / Anthropic / DeepMind tier:

- **Specialize visibly.** State your track: pretraining, post-training, RL, eval, agents, inference systems, infra. Generalist AI CVs lose to specialised ones.
- **"Memory math" and "failure modes"** are the things senior researchers test for in interviews. Surface evidence on the CV: papers replicated, benchmarks you understand, specific model behaviours you've debugged.
- **Don't list "ML projects" if they're Titanic / MNIST / Iris.** That actively *hurts* — signals you trained on tutorials. Show production-thinking projects: deployment, monitoring, real business framing.
- **Tools that signal seriousness for 2026**: PyTorch, HuggingFace, vLLM, LiteLLM, FastAPI, Docker, Kubernetes, MLflow, W&B, Ray. Listing TensorFlow alone without context now reads as "stopped learning around 2019."
- **Adversarial / eval / red-team work** is in unusually high demand. Specific contributors who have done deep eval work get pulled into Mercor, Surge, Scale AI's red-team functions, and frontier-lab internal eval teams.

---

## 8. Jane Street / quant-specific (since you mentioned them)

Jane Street's own published advice + the better third-party guides agree:

- **They read every application by hand.** No ATS to game. A real human looks at every CV — university name matters less than expected.
- **Quant pedigree first.** Math, stats, physics, CS coursework gets a "Math" section listing the heavy stuff: Real Analysis, Combinatorics, Stochastic Processes, Measure Theory. GPA 3.8+ goes prominently.
- **Competitions over coursework.** USAMO Qualifier, Putnam Top 500, Codeforces Candidate Master, IOI participation — these get *top* placement. Above work experience for early-career.
- **No cover letters.** They explicitly say they don't read them.
- **OCaml or Python explicit.** They don't expect OCaml going in, but listing it (with depth) is a real signal.
- **Project depth > project breadth.** "Implemented a compiler in OCaml" beats "Built a React Native to-do app" by a lot.

For HFT/MM more broadly (Optiver, IMC, HRT, Citadel, Jump, Two Sigma, DRW, Akuna): **C++ depth + low-latency systems experience + math background.** Resume needs to make the C++ visible — version (C++20/23), libraries (Boost, Folly, custom lock-free), concrete latency numbers.

---

## 9. Pet peeves that kill resumes (from hiring managers, ranked)

1. **Spelling/grammar errors.** After the first, many stop reading. Run multiple proofreads.
2. **Generic resumes.** A CV that could be sent to any role at any company signals you're spamming.
3. **No quantification anywhere.** All activity, no result.
4. **Skills lists that overstate.** Don't list a tool you can't whiteboard. Interviewers will probe specifically the things you over-listed.
5. **Inconsistent formatting.** Mixed bullet styles, mixed date formats, mixed tense, two different font weights — all read as "doesn't care."
6. **Photo on CV** (US/UK tech). Adds nothing; sometimes filtered out for bias-prevention reasons.
7. **An "Objective" or "Career Goals" section.** Replaced by Profile/Summary, but even those are increasingly contested. If kept, it must be specific and outcome-oriented.
8. **Two pages when one would do.** Two pages is acceptable for senior+ with substantive material — but never as padding.
9. **References available on request.** Universally implied; takes up a line.
10. **PDFs that crash ATS.** Plain ATS-compliant fonts, no tables, no images in the body, no two-column trickery for the version you submit. (A pretty version for human eyes is fine — but have an ATS-clean version too.)

---

## 10. The placement game — what goes where

The single biggest CV upgrade most engineers can make is **reordering**:

- **Top of page 1 (the F-pattern hot zone)**: name, current title, current company, one-line positioning statement, the top 2-3 skills/tools the role is hiring for, and the **strongest bullet you've ever written.**
- **Above the fold (top half of page 1)**: current role with its 2-3 strongest bullets.
- **Middle of page 1**: second-most-recent role.
- **Bottom of page 1**: older roles, with tighter bullets.
- **Page 2 (if it exists)**: education, side projects, awards, publications. Not core experience.

The reorder principle: **strongest material at the top of each section, weakest at the bottom.** This applies *within* a job entry too — first bullet hits 3.5× more eyeballs than the fourth.

---

## 11. Tailoring without rewriting the whole CV

The pros maintain **one master CV (2-3 pages, everything)** and **role-specific cuts (1 page)**. For each application:

1. Read the JD; pull out the 5-7 keywords that appear most.
2. Find the bullets in your master CV that already hit those keywords.
3. Reorder the chosen bullets so the strongest match is the first bullet of your current role.
4. Tweak the Profile (top 2-3 lines) to lead with the keyword cluster the JD uses.
5. Skills section: if it exists, reorder so JD-relevant tools are first.

Total time per application: 10-15 minutes after the master CV is built.

---

## 12. The "honest claim" doctrine

A pattern from senior hiring managers who interview a lot:

**Every line on a CV must survive 3 minutes of probing.** That means:
- Numbers must reconcile when asked how they were measured.
- "Led X" must hold up under "who reported to you and what decisions did you make?"
- "Designed Y" must survive "walk me through the design trade-offs you considered."
- Tools listed must survive whiteboard usage.

Anything that fails the 3-minute test is a net negative — better dropped than left to detonate in an interview.

---

# Resume and Cover Letter Writing Skill

Based on the SKILL.md documentation, here are the core instructions and frameworks:

## Key Framework: CAR Format
For achievement bullets, the skill uses: **Challenge** (context/problem), **Action** (what you did), **Result** (measurable outcome).

The guidance states: "Every bullet should answer: 'So what? What changed because of this?'"

## Resume Structure by Experience Level

**Entry-level (0-3 years):** Contact → Summary → Education → Experience → Skills → Certifications

**Mid-career (3-10 years):** Contact → Summary → Experience → Skills → Education → Certifications

**Senior (10+ years):** Contact → Executive Summary → Key Achievements → Experience → Board Roles → Education

## Action Verb Categories
The skill organizes verbs by contribution type—Leadership (Led, managed, mentored), Creation (Developed, launched, built), Improvement (Increased, streamlined, optimized), and Technical (Engineered, automated, deployed).

## Cover Letter Structure
Paragraph 1: "Opening hook—Why this role, why now, why you noticed"

Paragraph 2: Two to three specific experience-to-requirement matches using job listing language

Paragraph 3: Company-specific research showing genuine fit

Paragraph 4: Clear call to action

## ATS Compliance Requirements
"Use standard section headings...No tables, columns, or text boxes...No images, icons, or graphics...Standard fonts (Calibri, Arial, Garamond, Georgia)"

# claude-resume-kit: Core Methodology Extraction

## Anti-Fabrication Architecture

**Provenance tagging** marks every achievement with status flags:
- Published (peer-reviewed)
- Under review (submitted but unvetted)
- Internal (company/lab reports only)

**Verb discipline rules** prevent overclaiming. The system enforces constraints on action words—"contributed to" stays as-is rather than inflating to "developed" or "led."

**Corrections log** tracks fixes during review cycles, preventing reintroduced errors across resume iterations.

## AI Fingerprint Avoidance

The system implements:
- **Banned-word lists** targeting overused AI phrases ("leverage," "synergy," "paradigm")
- **Structural anti-patterns** (no 3+ bullets starting identically; varied sentence length)
- **Post-generation scan** (12-item checklist) evaluates output for human-readability markers before delivery

## Multi-Perspective Critique

Five reader personas score resumes across 8 dimensions in isolated Claude Code sessions:
1. ATS bot (keyword matching)
2. HR screener (role fit)
3. Hiring manager (impact narrative)
4. Technical reviewer (credibility)
5. Academic peer (publication weight)

Fresh context windows prevent bias accumulation.

## Workflow Separation

Each major step runs in **separate Claude Code sessions**:
- `/setup-extract` — paper analysis + structured Q&A
- `/setup-build-kb` — synthesis
- `/make-resume` — JD-tailored generation
- `/critique` — independent scoring
- `/edit-resume` — refinement loop

## LaTeX Template Structure

Templates use `[CONFIG: ...]` placeholders for:
- Fixed sections (education, header, awards)
- Dynamic injection points for experience bullets
- Publication lists with status annotations

## Knowledge Base Architecture

**Extraction → Experience files → Role-type bundles → Tailored output**

Extractions capture:
- Contribution scope (what you actually did)
- Publication status
- Domain keywords
- Quantifiable outcomes

Role-type bundles segment experience for academic vs. industry vs. startup contexts.

## Source Material Advantage

By extracting papers once with structured provenance metadata, the system avoids the "paste resume + paste JD" trap: it maintains a queryable knowledge base of *verified* claims rather than treating each application as a fresh rewrite opportunity.

# Resume Helper: Adversarial Multi-Agent Architecture

## The Four-Agent System

**Agent Roles & Information Access:**

| Agent | Role | Input Access | Purpose |
|-------|------|--------------|---------|
| **Writer** | Advocate | Raw experience, JD, current resume | Creates compelling resume draft |
| **Fact-Checker** | Validator | Raw experience, current resume | Verifies all claims against original input |
| **Interviewer** | Skeptic | Resume only (isolated) | Reviews like hiring manager would |
| **Coach** | Mediator | All sources + feedback | Synthesizes input, asks clarifying questions |

## Key Architectural Insight

The system enforces **information isolation**: *"The Interviewer never sees the candidate's raw input—just like a real hiring manager only sees the resume."* This creates authentic pressure testing.

## The Fact-Checker's Hallucination Prevention

The Fact-Checker prevents invented claims through:

1. **Direct verification** — *"Numbers, achievements, technologies, dates—all traced back to your input"*
2. **No embellishment** — If you provided "led team" without size, it stays vague rather than inventing "led team of 8"
3. **Three-strike rule** — Writer gets 3 attempts to fix hallucinations before escalating to user
4. **Fresh file reads** — Each iteration rereads original `working/inputs/` files directly

**Fact-Checker verdict options:** "PASS" or "FAIL"

## The Interviewer's Challenge Mechanism

The Interviewer provides **skeptical review** by:

- Reading *only* the resume (no context about candidate)
- Evaluating claims as a hiring manager would
- Issuing verdicts: "STRONG_CANDIDATE / NEEDS_WORK / RED_FLAGS"
- Feeding concerns to Coach without seeing raw justifications

## The Coach's Synthesis & Improvement Loop

The Coach:

1. **Aggregates parallel analysis** from vague-claims, buzzword, ATS, and quantification agents
2. **Asks clarifying questions** (team sizes, metrics, timelines, business impact)
3. **Issues verdicts**:
   - `READY` — Interview-ready, loop exits
   - `NEEDS_STRENGTHENING` — Too modest, add specifics
   - `NEEDS_GROUNDING` — Oversold, add evidence
   - `BLOCKED` — Missing info, ask user first

*"The Coach may need more information from you"* if resume doesn't converge.

## Hand-Off Pattern

```
Writer → Fact-Checker
  ↓ (Pass) 
Interviewer → Analysis Agents (parallel)
  ↓
Coach (synthesizes)
  ├→ READY (exit)
  └→ NOT READY (feedback → Writer, loop continues)
```

## File-Based Message Passing

Agents communicate through `working/` directory to prevent context exhaustion:
- Writer reads/writes `working/writer/output.md`
- Fact-Checker reads raw input, writes `working/fact_checker/verdict.md`
- Interviewer reads only resume draft
- Coach reads all verdicts, writes `working/coach/feedback.md` for next iteration

## Stealing This Methodology

**For your own adversarial system:**

1. **Enforce information isolation** — Different agents see different source material
2. **Use file-based state** — Prevents context window explosion in long loops
3. **Implement validation layer** — One agent specifically prevents hallucination
4. **Add skeptical review** — Agent evaluates output without full context
5. **Synthesize via coordinator** — Final agent reconciles contradictory feedback with user input
6. **Preserve user answers** — Save clarifications to input for future iterations

The genius is using *disagreement* (Writer vs. Interviewer) as a feature, not a bug.

# Stolen — ready to apply to your CV

## 🥇 Tier 1: Apply on the very next revision pass

### 1. **Provenance tagging** (from claude-resume-kit)
Every claim on your CV gets tagged with its evidence source in your private notes. Status flags:
- `verified-source` (came out of a repo / report / public artifact)
- `verified-dictation` (Sumeet said this in interrogation, defensible in interview)
- `inferred` (logical extension of source material, not directly stated)
- `unsourced` ← anything here gets cut or moved to "unverified, do not put on CV"

We've effectively already been doing this in the raw.md files. Now we formalise it: **every CV bullet should have a one-line provenance trail in a side doc.** If anyone challenges a bullet in interview, we know where it comes from.

### 2. **The "So what? What changed?" test** (from jezweb)
Their literal rule: *"Every bullet should answer: 'So what? What changed because of this?'"*

Apply to every bullet in the current draft. The CAR formula (Challenge / Action / Result) is just X-Y-Z restated — but the **"so what?"** phrasing is the cleanest mental check. If a bullet can't answer it in one sentence, the bullet is broken.

### 3. **The four-agent adversarial workflow** (from resume-helper)
We do this as a review pass *after* the next draft:

| Role | Sees | Verdict |
|------|------|---------|
| **Writer** | raw.md notes + job description + draft | produces bullets |
| **Fact-Checker** | raw.md notes + draft (NOT job description) | PASS / FAIL per bullet |
| **Interviewer** | draft only (NO raw.md) | STRONG_CANDIDATE / NEEDS_WORK / RED_FLAGS |
| **Coach** | all of the above + your input | READY / NEEDS_STRENGTHENING / NEEDS_GROUNDING / BLOCKED |

The genius: **the Interviewer never sees your justifications.** They review the resume the way a real hiring manager does — cold. Whatever doesn't stand up to that cold read gets revised.

We'll run this as a structured pass once we have a draft we both like.

### 4. **Three-strike rule on hallucinations**
If a bullet keeps drifting toward unsupported claims through revision, after 3 attempts to ground it → **cut the bullet entirely or escalate to you for clarification.** No "well it's mostly true" compromises. This is the rule that would have caught the Bristol Airport Prophet/89% problem before we did.

---

## 🥈 Tier 2: AI fingerprint avoidance (from claude-resume-kit)

This is critical — recruiters are increasingly pattern-matching on "this reads AI-generated."

### Banned-word list — kill on sight
- **leverage** ("leveraged X to do Y" → use "used X")
- **synergy / synergised / synergistic**
- **paradigm / paradigm shift**
- **robust / robustness** (when the context doesn't actually demand it — "built a robust system" → just "built a system" or specify what makes it robust)
- **comprehensive** (vague filler)
- **utilise / utilised** (use "used")
- **spearheaded** (use "led" or "drove")
- **stakeholders** (when generic — name them: "the data pipeline team", "the security org")
- **innovative / cutting-edge / state-of-the-art** (let the work speak)
- **passionate about** (filler)
- **deep dive / dove deep** (overused)
- **navigate / navigated** (as a metaphor — "navigated complex stakeholders" → say what you actually did)
- **landscape** (overused metaphor)
- **journey** (when describing a project)

### Structural anti-patterns — vary deliberately
- **No 3+ bullets starting with the same verb in a single role.** If you have "Built X / Built Y / Built Z" → rewrite at least one as "Re-architected", "Drove", "Designed".
- **Vary sentence length.** AI-generated text tends toward uniform-length sentences. Mix short punchy bullets with longer ones with subclauses.
- **No em-dash overuse.** Em-dashes are useful, but 4 em-dashes on a one-page CV reads as AI-generated. Cap at ~2 per CV.
- **No "not just X, but Y" / "X isn't just Y, it's Z" rhetorical structure.** Classic AI tell.

### 12-item post-generation human-readability checklist (assembled from the kit)
After drafting, run the CV through:

1. Any banned words present? Strip.
2. Three bullets starting with same verb? Vary.
3. More than 2 em-dashes? Reduce.
4. Any "not just X, but Y" structure? Rewrite.
5. Any sentence over 30 words? Break it.
6. All sentences roughly the same length? Vary.
7. Any abstract result ("preserving priority delivery") that doesn't say what concretely changed? Tighten.
8. Any tool listed that you can't defend in interview? Cut.
9. Any quantified claim that can't be sourced to a document or repo? Reframe or cut.
10. Any verb stronger than your actual role ("led" when you "contributed")? Downgrade.
11. Does the first bullet of your current role contain your single strongest result? If not, reorder.
12. Read aloud — any sentence sounds like a press release? Rewrite in plain English.

---

## 🥉 Tier 3: Five-reader scoring (from claude-resume-kit)

After the draft is solid, we score it from five personas in **separate context windows** (so opinions don't bleed):

1. **ATS bot** — keyword match score, formatting compatibility.
2. **HR screener** — does the role fit the listed JD? Are titles legible?
3. **Hiring manager** — is there a clear narrative? Do the results matter?
4. **Technical reviewer (peer)** — are the technical claims credible and defensible?
5. **Senior in the role you're applying for** — would you hire this person onto your team?

We can do this with the Agent tool — spawn 5 in parallel after we have a draft.

raw.md (✓ already done)

  → 4-agent adversarial review (Writer / Fact-Checker / Interviewer / Coach)
  → 5-persona scoring (parallel agents)
  → final draft
```
