The reading reality\n\nWhat's actually happening when a human reads a CV (eye-tracking studies, multiple sources):\n\n- **Time spent on first pass: ~7.4 seconds.**\n- **F-pattern reading:** top line across, down the left margin, partial scans across, more rapid descent.\n- **Six fixation points capture ~80% of attention:** name, current title, current company, dates of recent roles, education, top-of-page bullets.\n- **Dates, company names, and job titles get 67% more visual attention** than the bullets themselves.\n- The **yes/no decision is usually formed before a single bullet is read** — based on pattern-recognition signals: formatting quality, information density, visual hierarchy.\n- For tech roles, **GitHub links and certifications in the header get 60% more attention** than in other industries.\n- **The first bullet of each role is read 3.5× more often than the fourth.**\n\n**Implication:** the top third of page 1 is the entire CV in practice. Everything below is a tiebreaker. Your strongest, most quantified, most senior-signalling bullet should be the **first bullet of your current role.**\n\n---\n\n## 2. The X-Y-Z formula\n\nLaszlo Bock (ex-Google SVP People Ops) published this and it's the single most-cited bullet structure in modern tech CV advice:\n\n> **\"Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y] by doing [Z]\"**\n\n- **X** = the achievement (action verb)\n- **Y** = the quantified result\n- **Z** = the method / what you did\n\nExample progression:\n- Bad: *\"Worked on the search infrastructure.\"*\n- Better: *\"Improved search.\"*\n- X-Y-Z: *\"Improved search relevance (X) by 18% on the long-tail query distribution (Y) by replacing the BM25 ranker with a learned cross-encoder (Z).\"*\n\nThe formula forces leading with **what changed** instead of **what was touched**.\n\n### STAR vs X-Y-Z\n\nSTAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is the older, more verbose framework. On CV bullets, STAR is usually too long. X-Y-Z is the CV-density version of STAR. Most senior engineers don't have a \"Situation/Task\" worth spelling out — the role title does that. Skip to X-Y-Z.\n\n---\n\n## 3. Quantifying when you have no clean number\n\nThis is the hardest part of senior-eng CVs: the work is real but the metrics never existed. **Substitute outcome signals when you can't get a number:**\n\n- **Counterfactual** — *\"Built X — without which the Y release would have been blocked.\"*\n- **Selection / endorsement** — *\"Selected by [stakeholder] for [thing]\"*, *\"Recognised by [PMs] as [thing].\"* Borrows credibility from the stakeholder.\n- **First-of / before-after** — *\"IBM's first working rogue-AP detection across the Hursley estate.\"* The \"first working\" is the result.\n- **Audience scale** — *\"used by N services / N engineers / the platform team.\"*\n- **Authority granted** — *\"granted code-quality authority across the repo, authoring the 515-line standards the team enforces.\"*\n- **Permission unlocked** — *\"unblocked the firm's first ingest from the Indian market.\"*\n\n**Trap to avoid:** *\"enabled the team to ...\"* without saying what the team then did. Always close the loop.\n\n**Never make up a number.** \"Estimate when unavailable\" is bad advice. Use the substitution patterns above.\n\n---\n\n## 4. Verb hygiene\n\n### Kill these on sight\n- **\"Responsible for ...\"** — passive, scope-only, no result.\n- **\"Helped with ...\"**, **\"Assisted ...\"** — diminishes ownership.\n- **\"Worked on ...\"** — meaningless.\n- **\"Utilised ...\"** — pretentious \"used\".\n- **\"Various ...\"** — vagueness. Pick the specific ones.\n- **\"Successfully ...\"** — implied.\n- **\"Spearheaded ...\"** — overused buzzword.\n\n### Action verbs that age well\n- Led, Built, Designed, Shipped, Migrated, Rewrote, Cut, Reduced, Eliminated, Owned, Drove, Established, Authored, Re-architected.\n\n### Verb load-bearing by seniority signal\n- **Senior IC**: Built, Shipped, Cut, Migrated, Designed.\n- **Staff**: Owned, Drove, Established, Authored, Re-architected, Defined.\n- **Principal/Lead**: Drove, Established, Set, Decided, Chartered, Coached.\n\n### Verb discipline rule (stolen from claude-resume-kit)\nDon't inflate the verb beyond your actual role. *\"Contributed to\"* stays as-is rather than becoming *\"developed\"* or *\"led.\"* Stronger verb than your contribution = interview risk.\n\n---\n\n## 5. Senior vs Staff vs Principal scope signals\n\nSubtle but important distinction:\n\n- **Senior** — ownership *within a team's domain.* Bullets describe components shipped, features owned, individual systems built.\n- **Staff** — ownership *across teams.* Bullets describe initiatives that unblocked multiple teams, standards that propagated, architectures that defined how N services interact.\n- **Principal** — ownership *of an entire product area or organisation.* Bullets describe the technical direction the org now takes, the trade-offs made at scale, people coached into staff roles.\n\nIf you're applying for staff, the CV needs evidence that **your work touched things outside your immediate team's boundary**. Cross-team migrations, standards authored, platforms used by others, architecture decisions adopted org-wide.\n\nMost \"stuck at senior\" engineers have **excellent senior bullets** but no bullets that *prove they operated above their team*. That's the gap to fix.\n\n---\n\n## 6. Frontier-lab / AI-specific advice\n\nFrom Vlad Feinberg (ex-Google researcher) and the latest 2026 hiring guidance for OpenAI / Anthropic / DeepMind tier:\n\n- **Specialise visibly.** State your track: pretraining, post-training, RL, eval, agents, inference systems, infra. Generalist AI CVs lose to specialised ones.\n- **\"Memory math\" and \"failure modes\"** are what senior researchers test for in interviews. Surface evidence on the CV: papers replicated, benchmarks you understand, specific model behaviours you've debugged.\n- **Don't list \"ML projects\" if they're Titanic / MNIST / Iris.** Hurts more than helps — signals you trained on tutorials. Show production-thinking projects: deployment, monitoring, real business framing.\n- **Tools that signal seriousness for 2026**: PyTorch, HuggingFace, vLLM, LiteLLM, FastAPI, Docker, Kubernetes, MLflow, W&B, Ray. Listing TensorFlow alone now reads as \"stopped learning around 2019.\"\n- **Adversarial / eval / red-team work** is in unusually high demand. Specific contributors who have done deep eval work get pulled into Mercor, Surge, Scale AI's red-team, and frontier-lab internal eval teams.\n- **Total comp at senior level regularly exceeds $500K** at top frontier labs — worth knowing for negotiation framing.\n\n---\n\n## 7. Jane Street / quant-specific advice\n\nFrom Jane Street's published guidance and the better third-party prep guides:\n\n- **They read every application by hand.** No ATS to game.\n- **Quant pedigree first.** Math, stats, physics, CS coursework gets a \"Math\" section: Real Analysis, Combinatorics, Stochastic Processes, Measure Theory. GPA 3.8+ goes prominently.\n- **Competitions over coursework.** USAMO Qualifier, Putnam Top 500, Codeforces Candidate Master, IOI participation — top of CV.\n- **No cover letters.** Explicitly stated they don't read them.\n- **OCaml or Python explicit.** OCaml is optional but listing it (with depth) signals.\n- **Project depth > project breadth.** *\"Implemented a compiler in OCaml\"* beats *\"Built a React Native to-do app\"* by a lot.\n\nFor HFT/MM more broadly (Optiver, IMC, HRT, Citadel, Jump, Two Sigma, DRW, Akuna): **C++ depth + low-latency systems experience + math background.** Resume needs the C++ visible — version (C++20/23), libraries (Boost, Folly, custom lock-free), concrete latency numbers.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Pet peeves that kill resumes\n\nRanked, from hiring-manager surveys:\n\n1. **Spelling / grammar errors.** After the first, many stop reading.\n2. **Generic resumes.** A CV that could be sent to any role signals you're spamming.\n3. **No quantification anywhere.** All activity, no result.\n4. **Skills lists that overstate.** Don't list a tool you can't whiteboard. Interviewers will probe specifically the things you over-listed.\n5. **Inconsistent formatting.** Mixed bullet styles, mixed date formats, mixed tense — reads as \"doesn't care.\"\n6. **Photo on CV** (US/UK tech) — adds nothing; sometimes filtered for bias-prevention.\n7. **\"Objective\" or \"Career Goals\" section.** Replaced by Profile/Summary. If kept, must be specific.\n8. **Two pages when one would do.** Two pages acceptable for senior+ with substantive material; never as padding.\n9. **\"References available on request.\"** Universally implied; wastes a line.\n10. **PDFs that crash ATS.** Plain fonts, no tables, no images, no two-column trickery for the submitted version.\n\n---\n\n## 9. The placement game\n\nThe single biggest CV upgrade most engineers can make is **reordering:**\n\n- **Top of page 1 (F-pattern hot zone):** name, current title, current company, one-line positioning statement, top 2-3 skills/tools the role hires for, **strongest bullet you've ever written.**\n- **Above the fold:** current role with its 2-3 strongest bullets.\n- **Middle of page 1:** second-most-recent role.\n- **Bottom of page 1:** older roles, tighter bullets.\n- **Page 2 (if it exists):** education, side projects, awards, publications.\n\n**Reorder principle:** strongest material at the top of each section, weakest at the bottom. This applies *within* a job entry too — first bullet hits 3.5× more eyeballs than the fourth.\n\n---\n\n## 10. Tailoring without rewriting\n\nPros maintain **one master CV (2-3 pages, everything)** and **role-specific cuts (1 page).** For each application:\n\n1. Read the JD; pull the 5-7 keywords that appear most.\n2. Find the bullets in your master CV that already hit those keywords.\n3. Reorder so the strongest match is the first bullet of your current role.\n4. Tweak the Profile (top 2-3 lines) to lead with the keyword cluster the JD uses.\n5. Skills section: reorder so JD-relevant tools are first.\n\nTotal time per application: 10-15 minutes once the master CV is built.\n\n---\n\n## 11. The honest-claim doctrine\n\nA pattern from senior hiring managers who interview a lot:\n\n**Every line on a CV must survive 3 minutes of probing.** That means:\n- Numbers reconcile when asked how they were measured.\n- *\"Led X\"* holds up under *\"who reported to you and what decisions did you make?\"*\n- *\"Designed Y\"* survives *\"walk me through the design trade-offs you considered.\"*\n- Tools listed survive whiteboard usage.\n\nAnything that fails the 3-minute test is a net negative — better dropped than left to detonate in an interview.\n\nThis is the rule that catches things like the Bristol Airport Prophet/89% problem before they hit a CV.\n\n---\n\n## 12. Stolen — provenance and verb discipline\n\n**From `ARPeeketi/claude-resume-kit`** (LaTeX-native, anti-fabrication, AI-fingerprint avoidance).\n\n### Provenance tagging\nEvery claim on the CV gets tagged with its evidence source in private notes. Status flags:\n- `verified-source` — came out of a repo / report / public artifact\n- `verified-dictation` — said in interrogation, defensible in interview\n- `inferred` — logical extension of source material, not directly stated\n- `unsourced` — gets cut or moved to \"do not put on CV\"\n\n### Verb discipline\nDon't inflate the verb beyond your actual role. *\"Contributed to\"* stays. Stronger verb than actual contribution = interview risk.\n\n### Corrections log\nTrack fixes during review cycles. Prevents reintroducing already-deleted overclaims across iterations.\n\n### Knowledge base architecture\n**Extraction → Experience files → Role-type bundles → Tailored output.** Already implemented in our raw.md flow:\n- Extractions capture: contribution scope (what you actually did), publication status, domain keywords, quantifiable outcomes.\n- Role-type bundles segment experience for academic vs. industry vs. startup contexts.\n\n---\n\n## 13. Stolen — adversarial four-agent review\n\n**From `MadeByTokens/resume-helper`** (adversarial multi-agent honesty).\n\n### Agent roles and information access\n\n| Agent | Sees | Verdict |\n|-------|------|---------|\n| **Writer** | raw notes + JD + draft | produces bullets |\n| **Fact-Checker** | raw notes + draft (NOT job description) | PASS / FAIL per bullet |\n| **Interviewer** | draft ONLY (no raw notes) | STRONG_CANDIDATE / NEEDS_WORK / RED_FLAGS |\n| **Coach** | all of the above + user input | READY / NEEDS_STRENGTHENING / NEEDS_GROUNDING / BLOCKED |\n\n### The key architectural insight\n**The Interviewer never sees the candidate's raw input — just like a real hiring manager only sees the resume.** This creates authentic pressure testing.\n\n### Hand-off pattern\n```\nWriter → Fact-Checker\n  ↓ (Pass)\nInterviewer → Analysis Agents (parallel)\n  ↓\nCoach (synthesizes)\n  ├→ READY (exit)\n  └→ NOT READY (feedback → Writer, loop continues)\n```\n\n### Three-strike rule on hallucinations\nWriter gets 3 attempts to fix any fabricated claim before escalating to user. No \"well it's mostly true\" compromises.\n\n### File-based message passing\nAgents communicate through a `working/` directory to prevent context exhaustion. For us this means each adversarial pass writes its verdicts to disk so the next iteration can read them cleanly.\n\n---\n\n## 14. Stolen — \"so what?\" test\n\n**From `jezweb/claude-skills` resume-cover-letter SKILL.md.**\n\n> *\"Every bullet should answer: 'So what? What changed because of this?'\"*\n\nThe cleanest mental check. Apply to every bullet in any draft. If the answer takes more than one sentence, the bullet is broken.\n\n### CAR format (Challenge / Action / Result)\nEssentially X-Y-Z restated with explicit \"context\" instead of \"measurement.\" Both work; pick whichever phrasing is clearer for a given bullet.\n\n---\n\n## 15. AI fingerprint avoidance — banned words + anti-patterns\n\nRecruiters are increasingly pattern-matching on \"this reads AI-generated.\" Output that triggers it gets discarded silently.\n\n### Banned-word list — kill on sight\n\n| Word/phrase | Why it dies | Replace with |\n|-------------|-------------|--------------|\n| leverage / leveraged | classic AI tell | use, used |\n| synergy / synergised | dead corporate speak | (cut) |\n| paradigm / paradigm shift | overused | (cut, describe specifically) |\n| robust / robustness | vague filler | specify what makes it robust |\n| comprehensive | vague filler | (cut) |\n| utilise / utilised | pretentious | use, used |\n| spearheaded | overused | led, drove |\n| stakeholders (generic) | vague | name them: \"the data pipeline team\" |\n| innovative / cutting-edge / state-of-the-art | self-praise | let the work speak |\n| passionate about | filler | (cut) |\n| deep dive / dove deep | overused | (cut, be specific) |\n| navigate / navigated (metaphorical) | vague | say what you did |\n| landscape (metaphorical) | overused | (cut) |\n| journey | over-romantic | (cut) |\n| seamless / seamlessly | filler | (cut) |\n| at the forefront of | self-praise | (cut) |\n| best-in-class | self-praise | (cut) |\n\n### Structural anti-patterns\n\n- **No 3+ bullets starting with the same verb in a single role.** \"Built X / Built Y / Built Z\" → rewrite at least one as \"Re-architected\", \"Drove\", \"Designed\".\n- **Vary sentence length.** AI-generated text tends toward uniform-length sentences. Mix short punchy bullets with longer ones with subclauses.\n- **Em-dash discipline.** Em-dashes are useful but 4+ on a one-page CV reads as AI-generated. Cap at ~2.\n- **No \"not just X, but Y\" or \"X isn't just Y, it's Z\" rhetorical structure.** Classic AI tell.\n- **No tricolons / rule-of-three.** \"We delivered X, Y, and Z.\" AI overuses this. Vary.\n\n---\n\n## 16. The 12-item post-generation human-readability checklist\n\nRun the CV through this after every draft:\n\n1. Any banned words present? Strip.\n2. Three bullets starting with the same verb in one role? Vary.\n3. More than 2 em-dashes on the page? Reduce.\n4. Any *\"not just X, but Y\"* structure? Rewrite.\n5. Any sentence over 30 words? Break it.\n6. All sentences roughly the same length? Vary.\n7. Any abstract result (*\"preserving priority delivery\"*) that doesn't say what concretely changed? Tighten.\n8. Any tool listed that you can't defend in interview? Cut.\n9. Any quantified claim that can't be sourced to a document or repo? Reframe or cut.\n10. Any verb stronger than your actual role (*\"led\"* when you *\"contributed\"*)? Downgrade.\n11. Does the first bullet of your current role contain your single strongest result? If not, reorder.\n12. Read aloud — any sentence sounds like a press release? Rewrite in plain English.\n\n---\n\n## 17. Five-persona scoring (separate contexts)\n\nAfter the draft is solid, score it from five personas in **separate context windows** (so opinions don't bleed):\n\n1. **ATS bot** — keyword match score, formatting compatibility.\n2. **HR screener** — does the role fit? Are titles legible?\n3. **Hiring manager** — clear narrative? Do the results matter?\n4. **Technical reviewer (peer)** — are technical claims credible and defensible?\n5. **Senior in the role you're applying for** — would you hire this person onto your team?\n\nImplementation: spawn five agents in parallel after the draft is locked. Each persona scores independently. Reconcile contradictions through the Coach role.\n\n---\n\n## 18. The workflow\n\n```\nraw.md (per-project source notes — done)\n  → draft v1 (LaTeX resume.tex)\n  → \"so what?\" pass on every bullet\n  → AI fingerprint scan (12-item checklist + banned words)\n  → 4-agent adversarial review (Writer / Fact-Checker / Interviewer / Coach)\n  → 5-persona scoring (parallel agents)\n  → final draft\n  → role-tailored variants (10-15 min each, reorder/swap from master)\n```\n\n---\n\n## 19. Tools and scanners worth running\n\n### ATS scanners (machine-side)\n- **[Jobscan](https://www.jobscan.co/)** — pastes JD + CV, returns ATS keyword-match score. Industry standard for ATS optimisation.\n- **[Resume Worded](https://resumeworded.com/)** — automated CV scoring across 30+ checks; particularly good at flagging weak verb usage and quantification gaps.\n- **[Skillsyncer](https://skillsyncer.com/)** — ATS-style keyword matcher; sometimes catches things Jobscan misses.\n\n### Eye-tracking / scan-pattern analysers (human-side)\n- **[ResumeHeatMap](https://resumeheatmap.com/eye-tracking-study)** — published the 6-fixation-points study; offers an analyser tool that simulates F-pattern attention on your CV.\n- **[Resumly's AI scanner](https://www.resumly.ai/blog/how-to-simulate-recruiter-glance-using-eye-tracking-ai)** — simulates a recruiter's 7-second glance.\n\n### Readability / sentence-pattern\n- **[Hemingway Editor](https://hemingwayapp.com/)** — flags overlong sentences, passive voice, adverb overuse.\n- **[Grammarly](https://www.grammarly.com/)** — spelling, grammar, basic tone (premium has better tone analysis).\n\n### AI-text detectors (run your CV through to make sure it doesn't trigger them)\n- **[GPTZero](https://gptzero.me/)** — flags AI-generated text. If your CV trips GPTZero, recruiters' internal tools will probably trip too.\n- **[Originality.ai](https://originality.ai/)** — same purpose, different detection profile. Run both.\n\n### LaTeX-specific\n- **Overleaf** — if local TeX install isn't cooperating, Overleaf has every package and renders in-browser.\n- **[texdoc](https://texdoc.org/)** — quick access to package documentation.\n\n### Compensation research (for negotiation)\n- **[levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/)** — total comp by company, level, location.\n- **[Glassdoor](https://www.glassdoor.com/)** — salary data + company reviews.\n\n### Job board / company research\n- **[Mercor](https://mercor.com/)** — AI talent marketplace.\n- **[Hacker News Who's Hiring](https://news.ycombinator.com/jobs)** — monthly thread; high-signal early-stage / quant / AI roles.\n- **[Wellfound (AngelList Talent)](https://wellfound.com/)** — startup roles with equity transparency.\n\n---\n\n## 20. Section ordering by experience level\n\nFrom the jezweb resume-cover-letter skill — generally accepted hierarchy:\n\n| Career stage | Order |\n|--------------|-------|\n| **Entry-level (0–3 years)** | Contact → Summary → Education → Experience → Skills → Certifications |\n| **Mid-career (3–10 years)** | Contact → Summary → Experience → Skills → Education → Certifications |\n| **Senior (10+ years)** | Contact → Executive Summary → Key Achievements → Experience → Board Roles / Advisory → Education |\n\nThe pivot point: at 3+ years, **Experience moves above Education.** At senior+, a \"Key Achievements\" block before the Experience section becomes useful for surfacing the biggest wins in the F-pattern hot zone.\n\nException: **academic CVs** put Publications/Grants/Teaching above industry Experience even at senior level.\n\n---\n\n## 8. Skills section placement — the contested spot\n\nThis is the one area where sources disagree:\n\n- **FAANG hiring-manager school**: Skills section at the **top**, directly below contact info. Reasoning: hiring managers need to validate the tech stack before they invest reading time. The first F-pattern scan should hit \"yes, this person uses our stack.\"\n- **Traditional UK CV school**: Skills section at the **bottom**. Reasoning: skills are implicit in the experience bullets; a dedicated section reads as \"padding\".\n- **Quant / Jane Street school**: No traditional \"Skills\" section; quant pedigree is signalled through coursework and competitions.\n\n**Practical rule:**\n- If you have clear evidence of the JD's required stack in your experience bullets → bottom or omit.\n- If the JD names tools you've used but the bullets don't surface them visibly → keep skills section near the top.\n- For US tech / FAANG / startup roles → top.\n- For UK / academic / quant → bottom or omit.\n\n---\n\n## 9. Frontier-lab / AI-specific advice"
}

  "new_string": "## 12. ATS compliance specifics\n\nApplicant Tracking Systems can choke on formatting tricks. ~75% rejection rate makes this load-bearing. **The submitted-to-the-ATS version of the CV must follow these rules:**\n\n- **Standard section headings** — \"Experience\", \"Education\", \"Skills\". ATS pattern-matches on these literal words; clever rewording (\"My Journey\") confuses the parser.\n- **No tables.** ATS readers serialise tables incorrectly; cells become run-on text.\n- **No columns** (single-column layout only for the submitted version).\n- **No text boxes.**\n- **No images, icons, or graphics in the body.** (Photo in header also kills ATS parsing on top of the bias issue.)\n- **Standard fonts**: Calibri, Arial, Garamond, Georgia, Times. No display fonts.\n- **Real text, not text-rendered-as-image.**\n- **PDF format**, not Word (.docx) for submission unless explicitly requested. PDFs preserve layout; Word files re-flow.\n- **No headers/footers** on page 1 — many ATS parsers skip them.\n- **Use literal job titles** (\"Software Engineer\", not \"Code Wizard\").\n\n**Compromise pattern many engineers use**: maintain two versions:\n1. A *pretty version* for human-facing channels (LinkedIn / portfolio / direct email).\n2. An *ATS-clean version* (LaTeX with no fancy layout, standard fonts, single column) for online application portals.\n\nSumeet's LaTeX file is already mostly ATS-clean — single column, standard structure — so this is one CV, not two.\n\n---\n\n## 13. Regional CV format differences\n\n| Region | Photo | Length | Personal info | Tone |\n|--------|-------|--------|---------------|------|\n| **US** | No | 1 page (2 for senior+) | Email, phone, LinkedIn, GitHub | Direct, achievement-focused |\n| **UK** | No | 2 pages standard | Email, phone, sometimes city | Slightly more formal; \"Interests\" line common |\n| **EU (DE/FR/NL)** | Yes (often) | 2–3 pages | Birth date, nationality, photo common | Formal; gaps must be explained |\n| **AU/NZ** | No | 2–3 pages standard | Similar to UK; \"Selection criteria\" responses for gov roles | Direct |\n| **Academic (global)** | No | Unlimited (CV not resume) | Full publication list | Comprehensive, no marketing tone |\n\nFor Sumeet (UK-based, applying to US tech / Mercor): **1-page US-style is the right default**; UK 2-pager is acceptable for senior+ if there's substantive material to fill it.\n\n---\n\n## 14. Cover letter structure (when one is wanted)\n\nJane Street explicitly doesn't want one. Most US tech doesn't read them carefully. But some EU / academic / startup founder applications still expect one. Structure when needed:\n\n| Paragraph | Purpose | What's in it |\n|-----------|---------|--------------|\n| **1 — Opening hook** | \"Why this role, why now, why I noticed\" | A specific reason you applied to *this* company, not the role generically. |\n| **2 — Match evidence** | 2–3 specific experience-to-requirement matches | Use the JD's language; surface bullets from your CV with tighter framing. |\n| **3 — Company-specific research** | Show you've understood their business / product / culture | One concrete observation about the company that proves you've done homework. |\n| **4 — Clear CTA** | What you want to happen next | \"Happy to walk through X in a call\" — direct ask, no hedging. |\n\n**Length cap: half a page.** Anything longer is unread.\n\n**Modern alternative**: a short, dense LinkedIn message or a 3-bullet email body. Reads more often than a formal cover letter for tech roles.\n\n---\n\n## 15. The placement game"
}

  "new_string": "This is the rule that catches things like the Bristol Airport Prophet/89% problem before they hit a CV.\n\n---\n\n## 18. The fact-check-against-source-documents process\n\nThe Bristol Airport correction in this very project is the best illustration. The original public writeup claimed:\n\n- \"ML forecasting model using **Facebook Prophet**\"\n- \"**89% accuracy** in predicting parking demand 7 days ahead\"\n\nBoth wrong, both went uncaught for years because nobody had read the actual source PDFs. When we did, we found:\n\n- Framework was actually **AWS Forecast**, not Prophet.\n- \"89%\" appears nowhere in either the team report or the individual report.\n- Sumeet wasn't on the ML side of the team — he was on data + AWS pipeline.\n\n**The process that catches this:**\n\n1. **Locate the source documents** for every claim — repo, PR list, report PDF, archive, public spec.\n2. **Read them, don't summarise from memory.** Memory drifts. Source documents don't.\n3. **Grep for the specific numbers and tool names** before putting them on a CV.\n4. **If the source doesn't contain the claim, the claim doesn't go on the CV.** No exceptions. Reframe with what *is* in the source.\n5. **If the source contradicts you**, update the public writeup *first*, then update the CV.\n\nThe pattern: **public writeup → CV** in that order, with the writeup as the audit trail. If the CV ever drifts ahead of the writeup, you've created a fabrication risk.\n\n**Tooling that makes this tractable:**\n- `pdftotext -layout <file>.pdf` to extract content from old reports.\n- `grep -r` across project archives for specific numbers / tool names.\n- `gh pr list --author <you>` to enumerate your real contributions in a repo.\n- `git log --author=<you>` for commit-level provenance.\n\n---\n\n## 19. Stolen — provenance and verb discipline"
}

39	
40	## 1. The reading reality
41	
42	What's actually happening when a human reads a CV (eye-tracking studies, multiple sources):
43	
44	- **Time spent on first pass: ~7.4 seconds.**
45	- **F-pattern reading:** top line across, down the left margin, partial scans across, more rapid descent.
46	- **Six fixation points capture ~80% of attention:** name, current title, current company, dates of recent roles, education, top-of-page bullets.
47	- **Dates, company names, and job titles get 67% more visual attention** than the bullets themselves.
48	- The **yes/no decision is usually formed before a single bullet is read** — based on pattern-recognition signals: formatting quality, information density, visual hierarchy.
49	- For tech roles, **GitHub links and certifications in the header get 60% more attention** than in other industries.
50	- **The first bullet of each role is read 3.5× more often than the fourth.**
51	
52	**Implication:** the top third of page 1 is the entire CV in practice. Everything below is a tiebreaker. Your strongest, most quantified, most senior-signalling bullet should be the **first bullet of your current role.**
53	
54	---
55	
56	## 2. Industry stats worth knowing
57	
58	Useful to keep in mind when sizing how much each CV decision actually moves the needle:
59	
60	- **~75% of resumes are rejected by ATS** before a human ever sees them.
61	- **~250 applications** is the average per posted role at popular companies.
62	- **Quantified achievements yield ~40% more interviews** than non-quantified ones.
63	- **Optimised applications yield 2–3× more interviews** vs. generic.
64	- **Frontier-lab senior comp regularly exceeds $500K total comp** (OpenAI / Anthropic / DeepMind tier).
65	- **Eye-tracking studies put first-pass time at ~7.4 seconds.** Decision is often made *before* a single bullet is read.
66	- **First bullet of each role gets 3.5× more reads than the fourth.**
67	- **GitHub links / certifications in the header get 60% more attention** in tech roles vs. other industries.
68	
69	---
70	
71	## 3. The X-Y-Z formula
72	
73	Laszlo Bock (ex-Google SVP People Ops) published this and it's the single most-cited bullet structure in modern tech CV advice:
74	
75	> **"Accomplished [X] as measured by [Y] by doing [Z]"**
76	
77	- **X** = the achievement (action verb)
78	- **Y** = the quantified result
79	- **Z** = the method / what you did
80	
81	Example progression:
82	- Bad: *"Worked on the search infrastructure."*
83	- Better: *"Improved search."*
84	- X-Y-Z: *"Improved search relevance (X) by 18% on the long-tail query distribution (Y) by replacing the BM25 ranker with a learned cross-encoder (Z)."*
85	
86	The formula forces leading with **what changed** instead of **what was touched**.
87	
88	### STAR vs X-Y-Z
89	
90	STAR (Situation, Task, Action, Result) is the older, more verbose framework. On CV bullets, STAR is usually too long. X-Y-Z is the CV-density version of STAR. Most senior engineers don't have a "Situation/Task" worth spelling out — the role title does that. Skip to X-Y-Z.
91	
92	---
93	
94	## 4. Quantifying when you have no clean number
95	
96	This is the hardest part of senior-eng CVs: the work is real but the metrics never existed. **Substitute outcome signals when you can't get a number:**
97	
98	- **Counterfactual** — *"Built X — without which the Y release would have been blocked."*
99	- **Selection / endorsement** — *"Selected by [stakeholder] for [thing]"*, *"Recognised by [PMs] as [thing]."* Borrows credibility from the stakeholder.
100	- **First-of / before-after** — *"IBM's first working rogue-AP detection across the Hursley estate."* The "first working" is the result.
101	- **Audience scale** — *"used by N services / N engineers / the platform team."*
102	- **Authority granted** — *"granted code-quality authority across the repo, authoring the 515-line standards the team enforces."*
103	- **Permission unlocked** — *"unblocked the firm's first ingest from the Indian market."*
104	
105	**Trap to avoid:** *"enabled the team to ..."* without saying what the team then did. Always close the loop.
106	
107	**Never make up a number.** "Estimate when unavailable" is bad advice. Use the substitution patterns above.
108	
109	---
110	
111	## 5. Verb hygiene (with categorised action verbs)
112	
113	### Kill these on sight
114	- **"Responsible for ..."** — passive, scope-only, no result.
115	- **"Helped with ..."**, **"Assisted ..."** — diminishes ownership.
116	- **"Worked on ..."** — meaningless.
117	- **"Utilised ..."** — pretentious "used".
118	- **"Various ..."** — vagueness. Pick the specific ones.
119	- **"Successfully ..."** — implied.
120	- **"Spearheaded ..."** — overused buzzword.
121	
122	### Action verbs that age well — by category
123	
124	| Category | Verbs |
125	|----------|-------|
126	| **Leadership** | Led, drove, mentored, coached, chartered, sponsored, owned, established, defined |
127	| **Creation** | Built, designed, developed, launched, shipped, authored, architected, prototyped |
128	| **Improvement** | Cut, reduced, eliminated, accelerated, streamlined, hardened, refactored, optimised |
129	| **Migration / change** | Migrated, re-architected, rewrote, ported, replaced, consolidated, decoupled |
130	| **Technical execution** | Engineered, automated, deployed, instrumented, integrated, debugged, profiled |
131	| **Analysis / decision** | Investigated, measured, benchmarked, validated, prioritised, scoped, planned |
132	| **Communication** | Presented, documented, briefed, negotiated, persuaded, championed |
133	
134	### Verb load-bearing by seniority signal
135	- **Senior IC**: Built, Shipped, Cut, Migrated, Designed.
136	- **Staff**: Owned, Drove, Established, Authored, Re-architected, Defined.
137	- **Principal/Lead**: Drove, Established, Set, Decided, Chartered, Coached.
138	
139	### Verb discipline rule (stolen from claude-resume-kit)
140	Don't inflate the verb beyond your actual role. *"Contributed to"* stays as-is rather than becoming *"developed"* or *"led."* Stronger verb than your contribution = interview risk.
141	
142	---
143	
144	## 6. Senior vs Staff vs Principal scope signals
145	
146	Subtle but important distinction:
147	
148	- **Senior** — ownership *within a team's domain.* Bullets describe components shipped, features owned, individual systems built.
149	- **Staff** — ownership *across teams.* Bullets describe initiatives that unblocked multiple teams, standards that propagated, architectures that defined how N services interact.
150	- **Principal** — ownership *of an entire product area or organisation.* Bullets describe the technical direction the org now takes, the trade-offs made at scale, people coached into staff roles.
151	
152	If you're applying for staff, the CV needs evidence that **your work touched things outside your immediate team's boundary**. Cross-team migrations, standards authored, platforms used by others, architecture decisions adopted org-wide.
153	
154	Most "stuck at senior" engineers have **excellent senior bullets** but no bullets that *prove they operated above their team*. That's the gap to fix.
155	
156	---
157	
158	## 7. Section ordering by experience level
159	
160	From the jezweb resume-cover-letter skill — generally accepted hierarchy:
161	
162	| Career stage | Order |
163	|--------------|-------|
164	| **Entry-level (0–3 years)** | Contact → Summary → Education → Experience → Skills → Certifications |
165	| **Mid-career (3–10 years)** | Contact → Summary → Experience → Skills → Education → Certifications |
166	| **Senior (10+ years)** | Contact → Executive Summary → Key Achievements → Experience → Board Roles / Advisory → Education |
167	
168	The pivot point: at 3+ years, **Experience moves above Education.** At senior+, a "Key Achievements" block before the Experience section becomes useful for surfacing the biggest wins in the F-pattern hot zone.
169	
170	Exception: **academic CVs** put Publications/Grants/Teaching above industry Experience even at senior level.
171	
172	---
173	
174	## 8. Skills section placement — the contested spot
175	
176	This is the one area where sources disagree:
177	
178	- **FAANG hiring-manager school**: Skills section at the **top**, directly below contact info. Reasoning: hiring managers need to validate the tech stack before they invest reading time. The first F-pattern scan should hit "yes, this person uses our stack."
179	- **Traditional UK CV school**: Skills section at the **bottom**. Reasoning: skills are implicit in the experience bullets; a dedicated section reads as "padding".
180	- **Quant / Jane Street school**: No traditional "Skills" section; quant pedigree is signalled through coursework and competitions.
181	
182	**Practical rule:**
183	- If you have clear evidence of the JD's required stack in your experience bullets → bottom or omit.
184	- If the JD names tools you've used but the bullets don't surface them visibly → keep skills section near the top.
185	- For US tech / FAANG / startup roles → top.
186	- For UK / academic / quant → bottom or omit.
187	
188	---
189	
190	## 9. Frontier-lab / AI-specific advice
191	
192	From Vlad Feinberg (ex-Google researcher) and the latest 2026 hiring guidance for OpenAI / Anthropic / DeepMind tier:
193	
194	- **Specialise visibly.** State your track: pretraining, post-training, RL, eval, agents, inference systems, infra. Generalist AI CVs lose to specialised ones.
195	- **"Memory math" and "failure modes"** are what senior researchers test for in interviews. Surface evidence on the CV: papers replicated, benchmarks you understand, specific model behaviours you've debugged.
196	- **Don't list "ML projects" if they're Titanic / MNIST / Iris.** Hurts more than helps — signals you trained on tutorials. Show production-thinking projects: deployment, monitoring, real business framing.
197	- **Tools that signal seriousness for 2026**: PyTorch, HuggingFace, vLLM, LiteLLM, FastAPI, Docker, Kubernetes, MLflow, W&B, Ray. Listing TensorFlow alone now reads as "stopped learning around 2019."
198	- **Adversarial / eval / red-team work** is in unusually high demand. Specific contributors who have done deep eval work get pulled into Mercor, Surge, Scale AI's red-team, and frontier-lab internal eval teams.
199	- **Total comp at senior level regularly exceeds $500K** at top frontier labs — worth knowing for negotiation framing.
200	
201	---
202	
203	## 10. Jane Street / quant-specific advice
204	
205	From Jane Street's published guidance and the better third-party prep guides:
206	
207	- **They read every application by hand.** No ATS to game.
208	- **Quant pedigree first.** Math, stats, physics, CS coursework gets a "Math" section: Real Analysis, Combinatorics, Stochastic Processes, Measure Theory. GPA 3.8+ goes prominently.
209	- **Competitions over coursework.** USAMO Qualifier, Putnam Top 500, Codeforces Candidate Master, IOI participation — top of CV.
210	- **No cover letters.** Explicitly stated they don't read them.
211	- **OCaml or Python explicit.** OCaml is optional but listing it (with depth) signals.
212	- **Project depth > project breadth.** *"Implemented a compiler in OCaml"* beats *"Built a React Native to-do app"* by a lot.
213	
214	For HFT/MM more broadly (Optiver, IMC, HRT, Citadel, Jump, Two Sigma, DRW, Akuna): **C++ depth + low-latency systems experience + math background.** Resume needs the C++ visible — version (C++20/23), libraries (Boost, Folly, custom lock-free), concrete latency numbers.
215	
216	---
217	
218	## 11. Pet peeves that kill resumes
219	
220	Ranked, from hiring-manager surveys:
221	
222	1. **Spelling / grammar errors.** After the first, many stop reading.
223	2. **Generic resumes.** A CV that could be sent to any role signals you're spamming.
224	3. **No quantification anywhere.** All activity, no result.
225	4. **Skills lists that overstate.** Don't list a tool you can't whiteboard. Interviewers will probe specifically the things you over-listed.
226	5. **Inconsistent formatting.** Mixed bullet styles, mixed date formats, mixed tense — reads as "doesn't care."
227	6. **Photo on CV** (US/UK tech) — adds nothing; sometimes filtered for bias-prevention.
228	7. **"Objective" or "Career Goals" section.** Replaced by Profile/Summary. If kept, must be specific.
229	8. **Two pages when one would do.** Two pages acceptable for senior+ with substantive material; never as padding.
230	9. **"References available on request."** Universally implied; wastes a line.
231	10. **PDFs that crash ATS.** Plain fonts, no tables, no images, no two-column trickery for the submitted version.
232	
233	---
234	
235	## 12. ATS compliance specifics
236	
237	Applicant Tracking Systems can choke on formatting tricks. ~75% rejection rate makes this load-bearing. **The submitted-to-the-ATS version of the CV must follow these rules:**
238	
239	- **Standard section headings** — "Experience", "Education", "Skills". ATS pattern-matches on these literal words; clever rewording ("My Journey") confuses the parser.
240	- **No tables.** ATS readers serialise tables incorrectly; cells become run-on text.
241	- **No columns** (single-column layout only for the submitted version).
242	- **No text boxes.**
243	- **No images, icons, or graphics in the body.** (Photo in header also kills ATS parsing on top of the bias issue.)
244	- **Standard fonts**: Calibri, Arial, Garamond, Georgia, Times. No display fonts.
245	- **Real text, not text-rendered-as-image.**
246	- **PDF format**, not Word (.docx) for submission unless explicitly requested. PDFs preserve layout; Word files re-flow.
247	- **No headers/footers** on page 1 — many ATS parsers skip them.
248	- **Use literal job titles** ("Software Engineer", not "Code Wizard").
249	
250	**Compromise pattern many engineers use**: maintain two versions:
251	1. A *pretty version* for human-facing channels (LinkedIn / portfolio / direct email).
252	2. An *ATS-clean version* (LaTeX with no fancy layout, standard fonts, single column) for online application portals.
253	
254	Sumeet's LaTeX file is already mostly ATS-clean — single column, standard structure — so this is one CV, not two.
255	
256	---
257	
258	## 13. Regional CV format differences
259	
260	| Region | Photo | Length | Personal info | Tone |
261	|--------|-------|--------|---------------|------|
262	| **US** | No | 1 page (2 for senior+) | Email, phone, LinkedIn, GitHub | Direct, achievement-focused |
263	| **UK** | No | 2 pages standard | Email, phone, sometimes city | Slightly more formal; "Interests" line common |
264	| **EU (DE/FR/NL)** | Yes (often) | 2–3 pages | Birth date, nationality, photo common | Formal; gaps must be explained |
265	| **AU/NZ** | No | 2–3 pages standard | Similar to UK; "Selection criteria" responses for gov roles | Direct |
266	| **Academic (global)** | No | Unlimited (CV not resume) | Full publication list | Comprehensive, no marketing tone |
267	
268	For Sumeet (UK-based, applying to US tech / Mercor): **1-page US-style is the right default**; UK 2-pager is acceptable for senior+ if there's substantive material to fill it.
269	
270	---
271	
272	## 14. Cover letter structure (when one is wanted)
273	
274	Jane Street explicitly doesn't want one. Most US tech doesn't read them carefully. But some EU / academic / startup founder applications still expect one. Structure when needed:
275	
276	| Paragraph | Purpose | What's in it |
277	|-----------|---------|--------------|
278	| **1 — Opening hook** | "Why this role, why now, why I noticed" | A specific reason you applied to *this* company, not the role generically. |
279	| **2 — Match evidence** | 2–3 specific experience-to-requirement matches | Use the JD's language; surface bullets from your CV with tighter framing. |
280	| **3 — Company-specific research** | Show you've understood their business / product / culture | One concrete observation about the company that proves you've done homework. |
281	| **4 — Clear CTA** | What you want to happen next | "Happy to walk through X in a call" — direct ask, no hedging. |
282	
283	**Length cap: half a page.** Anything longer is unread.
284	
285	**Modern alternative**: a short, dense LinkedIn message or a 3-bullet email body. Reads more often than a formal cover letter for tech roles.
286	
287	---
288	
289	## 15. The placement game
290	
291	The single biggest CV upgrade most engineers can make is **reordering:**
292	
293	- **Top of page 1 (F-pattern hot zone):** name, current title, current company, one-line positioning statement, top 2-3 skills/tools the role hires for, **strongest bullet you've ever written.**
294	- **Above the fold:** current role with its 2-3 strongest bullets.
295	- **Middle of page 1:** second-most-recent role.
296	- **Bottom of page 1:** older roles, tighter bullets.
297	- **Page 2 (if it exists):** education, side projects, awards, publications.
298	
299	**Reorder principle:** strongest material at the top of each section, weakest at the bottom. This applies *within* a job entry too — first bullet hits 3.5× more eyeballs than the fourth.
300	
301	---
302	
303	## 16. Tailoring without rewriting
304	
305	Pros maintain **one master CV (2-3 pages, everything)** and **role-specific cuts (1 page).** For each application:
306	
307	1. Read the JD; pull the 5-7 keywords that appear most.
308	2. Find the bullets in your master CV that already hit those keywords.
309	3. Reorder so the strongest match is the first bullet of your current role.
310	4. Tweak the Profile (top 2-3 lines) to lead with the keyword cluster the JD uses.
311	5. Skills section: reorder so JD-relevant tools are first.
312	
313	Total time per application: 10-15 minutes once the master CV is built.
314	
315	---
316	
317	## 17. The honest-claim doctrine
318	
319	A pattern from senior hiring managers who interview a lot:
320	
321	**Every line on a CV must survive 3 minutes of probing.** That means:
322	- Numbers reconcile when asked how they were measured.
323	- *"Led X"* holds up under *"who reported to you and what decisions did you make?"*
324	- *"Designed Y"* survives *"walk me through the design trade-offs you considered."*
325	- Tools listed survive whiteboard usage.
326	
327	Anything that fails the 3-minute test is a net negative — better dropped than left to detonate in an interview.
328	
329	This is the rule that catches things like the Bristol Airport Prophet/89% problem before they hit a CV.
330	
331	---
332	
333	## 18. The fact-check-against-source-documents process
334	
335	The Bristol Airport correction in this very project is the best illustration. The original public writeup claimed:
336	
337	- "ML forecasting model using **Facebook Prophet**"
338	- "**89% accuracy** in predicting parking demand 7 days ahead"
339	
340	Both wrong, both went uncaught for years because nobody had read the actual source PDFs. When we did, we found:
341	
342	- Framework was actually **AWS Forecast**, not Prophet.
343	- "89%" appears nowhere in either the team report or the individual report.
344	- Sumeet wasn't on the ML side of the team — he was on data + AWS pipeline.
345	
346	**The process that catches this:**
347	
348	1. **Locate the source documents** for every claim — repo, PR list, report PDF, archive, public spec.
349	2. **Read them, don't summarise from memory.** Memory drifts. Source documents don't.
350	3. **Grep for the specific numbers and tool names** before putting them on a CV.
351	4. **If the source doesn't contain the claim, the claim doesn't go on the CV.** No exceptions. Reframe with what *is* in the source.
352	5. **If the source contradicts you**, update the public writeup *first*, then update the CV.
353	
354	The pattern: **public writeup → CV** in that order, with the writeup as the audit trail. If the CV ever drifts ahead of the writeup, you've created a fabrication risk.
355	
356	**Tooling that makes this tractable:**
357	- `pdftotext -layout <file>.pdf` to extract content from old reports.
358	- `grep -r` across project archives for specific numbers / tool names.
359	- `gh pr list --author <you>` to enumerate your real contributions in a repo.
360	- `git log --author=<you>` for commit-level provenance.
361	
362	---
363	
364	## 19. Stolen — provenance and verb discipline
365	
366	**From `ARPeeketi/claude-resume-kit`** (LaTeX-native, anti-fabrication, AI-fingerprint avoidance).
367	
368	### Provenance tagging
369	Every claim on the CV gets tagged with its evidence source in private notes. Status flags:
370	- `verified-source` — came out of a repo / report / public artifact
371	- `verified-dictation` — said in interrogation, defensible in interview
372	- `inferred` — logical extension of source material, not directly stated
373	- `unsourced` — gets cut or moved to "do not put on CV"
374	
375	### Verb discipline
376	Don't inflate the verb beyond your actual role. *"Contributed to"* stays. Stronger verb than actual contribution = interview risk.
377	
378	### Corrections log
379	Track fixes during review cycles. Prevents reintroducing already-deleted overclaims across iterations.
380	
381	### Knowledge base architecture
382	**Extraction → Experience files → Role-type bundles → Tailored output.** Already implemented in our raw.md flow:
383	- Extractions capture: contribution scope (what you actually did), publication status, domain keywords, quantifiable outcomes.
384	- Role-type bundles segment experience for academic vs. industry vs. startup contexts.
385	
386	---
387	
388	## 20. Stolen — adversarial four-agent review
389	
390	**From `MadeByTokens/resume-helper`** (adversarial multi-agent honesty).
391	
392	### Agent roles and information access
393	
394	| Agent | Sees | Verdict |
395	|-------|------|---------|
396	| **Writer** | raw notes + JD + draft | produces bullets |
397	| **Fact-Checker** | raw notes + draft (NOT job description) | PASS / FAIL per bullet |
398	| **Interviewer** | draft ONLY (no raw notes) | STRONG_CANDIDATE / NEEDS_WORK / RED_FLAGS |
399	| **Coach** | all of the above + user input | READY / NEEDS_STRENGTHENING / NEEDS_GROUNDING / BLOCKED |
400	
401	### The key architectural insight
402	**The Interviewer never sees the candidate's raw input — just like a real hiring manager only sees the resume.** This creates authentic pressure testing.
403	
404	### Hand-off pattern
405	```
406	Writer → Fact-Checker
407	  ↓ (Pass)
408	Interviewer → Analysis Agents (parallel)
409	  ↓
410	Coach (synthesizes)
411	  ├→ READY (exit)
412	  └→ NOT READY (feedback → Writer, loop continues)
413	```
414	
415	### Three-strike rule on hallucinations
416	Writer gets 3 attempts to fix any fabricated claim before escalating to user. No "well it's mostly true" compromises.
417	
418	### File-based message passing
419	Agents communicate through a `working/` directory to prevent context exhaustion. For us this means each adversarial pass writes its verdicts to disk so the next iteration can read them cleanly.
420	
421	---
422	
423	## 21. Stolen — "so what?" test
424	
425	**From `jezweb/claude-skills` resume-cover-letter SKILL.md.**
426	
427	> *"Every bullet should answer: 'So what? What changed because of this?'"*
428	
429	The cleanest mental check. Apply to every bullet in any draft. If the answer takes more than one sentence, the bullet is broken.
430	
431	### CAR format (Challenge / Action / Result)
432	Essentially X-Y-Z restated with explicit "context" instead of "measurement." Both work; pick whichever phrasing is clearer for a given bullet.
433	
434	---
435	
436	## 22. AI fingerprint avoidance — banned words + anti-patterns
437	
438	Recruiters are increasingly pattern-matching on "this reads AI-generated." Output that triggers it gets discarded silently.
439	
440	### Banned-word list — kill on sight
441	
442	| Word/phrase | Why it dies | Replace with |
443	|-------------|-------------|--------------|
444	| leverage / leveraged | classic AI tell | use, used |
445	| synergy / synergised | dead corporate speak | (cut) |
446	| paradigm / paradigm shift | overused | (cut, describe specifically) |
447	| robust / robustness | vague filler | specify what makes it robust |
448	| comprehensive | vague filler | (cut) |
449	| utilise / utilised | pretentious | use, used |
450	| spearheaded | overused | led, drove |
451	| stakeholders (generic) | vague | name them: "the data pipeline team" |
452	| innovative / cutting-edge / state-of-the-art | self-praise | let the work speak |
453	| passionate about | filler | (cut) |
454	| deep dive / dove deep | overused | (cut, be specific) |
455	| navigate / navigated (metaphorical) | vague | say what you did |
456	| landscape (metaphorical) | overused | (cut) |
457	| journey | over-romantic | (cut) |
458	| seamless / seamlessly | filler | (cut) |
459	| at the forefront of | self-praise | (cut) |
460	| best-in-class | self-praise | (cut) |
461	
462	### Structural anti-patterns
463	
464	- **No 3+ bullets starting with the same verb in a single role.** "Built X / Built Y / Built Z" → rewrite at least one as "Re-architected", "Drove", "Designed".
465	- **Vary sentence length.** AI-generated text tends toward uniform-length sentences. Mix short punchy bullets with longer ones with subclauses.
466	- **Em-dash discipline.** Em-dashes are useful but 4+ on a one-page CV reads as AI-generated. Cap at ~2.
467	- **No "not just X, but Y" or "X isn't just Y, it's Z" rhetorical structure.** Classic AI tell.
468	- **No tricolons / rule-of-three.** "We delivered X, Y, and Z." AI overuses this. Vary.
469	
470	---
471	
472	## 23. The 12-item post-generation human-readability checklist
473	
474	Run the CV through this after every draft:
475	
476	1. Any banned words present? Strip.
477	2. Three bullets starting with the same verb in one role? Vary.
478	3. More than 2 em-dashes on the page? Reduce.
479	4. Any *"not just X, but Y"* structure? Rewrite.
480	5. Any sentence over 30 words? Break it.
481	6. All sentences roughly the same length? Vary.
482	7. Any abstract result (*"preserving priority delivery"*) that doesn't say what concretely changed? Tighten.
483	8. Any tool listed that you can't defend in interview? Cut.
484	9. Any quantified claim that can't be sourced to a document or repo? Reframe or cut.
485	10. Any verb stronger than your actual role (*"led"* when you *"contributed"*)? Downgrade.
486	11. Does the first bullet of your current role contain your single strongest result? If not, reorder.
487	12. Read aloud — any sentence sounds like a press release? Rewrite in plain English.
488	
489	---
490	
491	## 24. Five-persona scoring (separate contexts)
492	
493	After the draft is solid, score it from five personas in **separate context windows** (so opinions don't bleed):
494	
495	1. **ATS bot** — keyword match score, formatting compatibility.
496	2. **HR screener** — does the role fit? Are titles legible?
497	3. **Hiring manager** — clear narrative? Do the results matter?
498	4. **Technical reviewer (peer)** — are technical claims credible and defensible?
499	5. **Senior in the role you're applying for** — would you hire this person onto your team?
500	
501	Implementation: spawn five agents in parallel after the draft is locked. Each persona scores independently. Reconcile contradictions through the Coach role.
502	
503	---
504	
505	## 25. The workflow
506	
507	```
508	1. Source extraction
509	   - For every project / role on the CV: locate the actual source documents
510	     (repo + PR history + git log + report PDFs + protocol docs + dictation).
511	   - Run pdftotext, grep, gh pr list as needed.
512	   - Write raw.md per project capturing verbatim dictation + facts from sources.
513	
514	2. Fact-check the public writeup
515	   - If any public writeup (portfolio site, blog, LinkedIn) makes claims that
516	     don't appear in source documents, FIX THE WRITEUP FIRST.
517	   - The CV cannot drift ahead of the public writeup. The writeup is the audit trail.
518	
519	3. Draft v1
520	   - LaTeX resume.tex, ATS-clean, single column.
521	   - Each bullet draws only from raw.md provenance-tagged facts.
522	
523	4. The "so what?" pass
524	   - For every bullet: does it answer "so what? what changed because of this?"
525	   - If no, rewrite or cut.
526	
527	5. AI fingerprint scan
528	   - Run the 12-item checklist.
529	   - Strip banned words.
530	   - Vary verbs, sentence lengths, em-dash usage.
531	
532	6. Four-agent adversarial review
533	   - Writer → Fact-Checker → Interviewer → Coach.
534	   - Information isolation enforced — Interviewer sees CV only, no raw notes.
535	   - Three-strike rule on hallucinations.
536	
537	7. Five-persona scoring (parallel)
538	   - ATS bot / HR screener / hiring manager / technical peer / senior in target role.
539	   - Separate context windows to prevent bias bleed.
540	
541	8. Final draft
542	
543	9. Role-tailored variants
544	   - 10–15 min each.
545	   - Reorder bullets, tweak Profile to match JD keyword cluster, reorder Skills.
546	   - Master CV stays unchanged; variants live as separate files.
547	```

551	## 26. Tools and scanners worth running
552	
553	### ATS scanners (machine-side)
554	- **[Jobscan](https://www.jobscan.co/)** — pastes JD + CV, returns ATS keyword-match score. Industry standard for ATS optimisation.
555	- **[Resume Worded](https://resumeworded.com/)** — automated CV scoring across 30+ checks; particularly good at flagging weak verb usage and quantification gaps.
556	- **[Skillsyncer](https://skillsyncer.com/)** — ATS-style keyword matcher; sometimes catches things Jobscan misses.
557	
558	### Eye-tracking / scan-pattern analysers (human-side)
559	- **[ResumeHeatMap](https://resumeheatmap.com/eye-tracking-study)** — published the 6-fixation-points study; offers an analyser tool that simulates F-pattern attention on your CV.
560	- **[Resumly's AI scanner](https://www.resumly.ai/blog/how-to-simulate-recruiter-glance-using-eye-tracking-ai)** — simulates a recruiter's 7-second glance.
561	
562	### Readability / sentence-pattern
563	- **[Hemingway Editor](https://hemingwayapp.com/)** — flags overlong sentences, passive voice, adverb overuse.
564	- **[Grammarly](https://www.grammarly.com/)** — spelling, grammar, basic tone (premium has better tone analysis).
565	
566	### AI-text detectors (run your CV through to make sure it doesn't trigger them)
567	- **[GPTZero](https://gptzero.me/)** — flags AI-generated text. If your CV trips GPTZero, recruiters' internal tools will probably trip too.
568	- **[Originality.ai](https://originality.ai/)** — same purpose, different detection profile. Run both.
569	
570	### LaTeX-specific
571	- **Overleaf** — if local TeX install isn't cooperating, Overleaf has every package and renders in-browser.
572	- **[texdoc](https://texdoc.org/)** — quick access to package documentation.
573	
574	### Compensation research (for negotiation)
575	- **[levels.fyi](https://www.levels.fyi/)** — total comp by company, level, location.
576	- **[Glassdoor](https://www.glassdoor.com/)** — salary data + company reviews.
577	
578	### Job board / company research
579	- **[Mercor](https://mercor.com/)** — AI talent marketplace.
580	- **[Hacker News Who's Hiring](https://news.ycombinator.com/jobs)** — monthly thread; high-signal early-stage / quant / AI roles.
581	- **[Wellfound (AngelList Talent)](https://wellfound.com/)** — startup roles with equity transparency.

584	
585	## 27. Miscellaneous practical details
586	
587	### Profile / Summary block — what each line should do
588	
589	A strong 3–4 line Profile follows this template:
590	
591	| Line | Purpose |
592	|------|---------|
593	| **1** | Positioning claim — one sentence that says what kind of engineer you are. Lead with the strongest noun, not "I am..." |
594	| **2** | Current role + the single biggest thing you're doing right now (with a concrete outcome or stakeholder). |
595	| **3** | One-sentence prior career arc — 2-3 most credible previous roles compressed, each with a one-phrase outcome attached. |
596	| **4** | Credential / school / certification line (optional, often only needed if the rest of the CV doesn't surface it). |
597	
598	Avoid: "Passionate about...", "I am a...", "Looking for opportunities to...". These signal entry-level.
599	
600	### "Fewer strong bullets > more weak ones" — explicit principle
601	
602	Across every reviewed source, this is the single most consistent senior-eng advice. Two bullets that survive 3-minute probing beat five bullets that don't. **If a role has only 2 strong bullets, use 2.** Padding with weaker third/fourth bullets *lowers* the perceived quality of the whole entry because the eye-tracking studies show those positions get diminishing attention anyway — and any weak bullet sets the impression for the role.
603	
604	### ATS keyword match score targets
605	
606	- **Jobscan's threshold**: 75–80% match against the JD is considered "well-tailored."
607	- **Below 60%** generally won't pass the ATS filter at most large companies.
608	- The match isn't just keyword presence — context matters. Listing "Python" in a Skills section counts less than using "Python" inside a results-oriented bullet.
609	
610	**Practical workflow**: paste each new JD into Jobscan, score the CV, identify the top 5 missing keywords, see whether any can be honestly woven into existing bullets without fabrication. If they can't, the JD likely isn't a good match.
611	
612	### CV file naming convention
613	
614	- **Right**: `Sumeet_Saini_Resume_2026.pdf`, `Sumeet_Saini_CV.pdf`, `SumeetSaini_Mercor.pdf`.
615	- **Wrong**: `resume_final_v3_REAL.pdf`, `MyResume.pdf`, `Untitled.pdf`, `Sumeet.pdf`.
616	- For company-tailored variants: `Sumeet_Saini_Resume_<Company>.pdf` (lets recruiters see at-a-glance which version they have).
617	
618	### LinkedIn / CV sync
619	
620	The CV and LinkedIn must agree on:
621	- **Job titles** — exact match. "Tech Lead" on LinkedIn but "Founding Engineer" on CV reads as fabrication.
622	- **Employment dates** — must match to the month.
623	- **Company names** — exact.
624	- **Education** — degree name, institution, dates.
625	
626	The CV can be *tighter* than LinkedIn (LinkedIn often has more bullets, the full job history, etc.) but never *contradictory*. A recruiter cross-referencing the two should find no surprises.
627	
628	### "Borrowed impact" framing
629	
630	When the metrics belong to a downstream team or product but your work enabled them, attribute the work transparently:
631	
632	- "Built the data pipeline used by the strategy team to develop their first NSE trading models." (Your work + their use, no fabrication.)
633	- "Authored the code-quality standards that govern all PRs merged into the codebase across the team." (Your output + adopted scope.)
634	- "Designed the auth layer that gates access for every prospect in the demo environment." (Your work + concrete downstream use.)
635	
636	Versus the fabricated/inflated version:

## Proposed plan: build the master CV from scratch, then derive variants

### Phase 0 — Setup (5 min)
- New file structure under `/Users/sumeet/Documents/work/resume/resume_tex/`:
  - `resume_master.tex` — the 2-page everything-CV (audit trail)
  - `resume_mercor.tex` — the first 1-page variant
  - `variants/<company>.tex` — future variants
  - Keep the current `resume.tex` as `resume_legacy_2024.tex` for reference
- Move `CV_METHODOLOGY.md` and `raw.md` references → these stay as is.

### Phase 1 — Master CV draft (the hard work)
Build it **bottom-up**: write the bullets first, then let the Profile fall out of them. Each bullet must:
- Answer "so what?" in one sentence (§21).
- Source-trace to a `raw.md` entry (§19 provenance tagging).
- Use a verb honest to your actual role (§19 verb discipline).
- Avoid every banned word in §22.
- Use one of the §4 quantification patterns (counterfactual / endorsement / first-of / audience-scale / authority-granted / permission-unlocked) when there's no clean number.

Order I'd build in:
1. Header (name + contact + GitHub).
2. Experience entries — bottom-up, roles in reverse chronological order:
   - Tech Lead, Stealth AI Startup
   - AI Training Contractor
   - Mako (3 bullets max, strongest first)
   - KCL Research Assistant (1 bullet)
   - IBM (2 bullets)
3. Education (dissertation + Bristol Airport corrected).
4. Extracurriculars (KCL AI Soc, hackathons, London Financial).
5. Skills (modular — can be reordered or omitted per variant).
6. Interests (kept, UK convention).
7. **Profile written last** — derived from the strongest material above.

### Phase 2 — Run the methodology passes (in order)
- §21 "so what?" pass on every bullet.
- §22 AI fingerprint scan (banned words, structural anti-patterns).
- §23 12-item human-readability checklist.

### Phase 3 — Four-agent adversarial review (§20)
Spawn four agents in parallel:
- **Writer** sees raw.md + JD + draft.
- **Fact-Checker** sees raw.md + draft. PASS / FAIL per bullet.
- **Interviewer** sees the draft only. STRONG / NEEDS_WORK / RED_FLAGS.
- **Coach** synthesises. READY / NEEDS_STRENGTHENING / NEEDS_GROUNDING / BLOCKED.

Iterate until READY. Three-strike rule on any flagged hallucination.

### Phase 4 — Five-persona scoring (§24)
Spawn five agents in parallel, each in a fresh context:
- ATS bot
- HR screener
- Hiring manager
- Technical peer
- Senior in the target role

Each scores independently. Reconcile contradictions.

### Phase 5 — Lock the master, build the Mercor variant
- Master stays 2 pages, holds everything.
- Mercor variant: 1-page cut, reordered to lead with AI training + Tech Lead, Profile rewritten to use Mercor's domain language.

### Phase 6 — Tailoring framework
Two options:
- **Simple**: copy `resume_master.tex` → `resume_<company>.tex` per application, cut from there. Works fine, slight file proliferation.
- **Sophisticated**: adopt the `[CONFIG: ...]` placeholder pattern from §27. One LaTeX source + per-target YAML configs. More setup cost, cheaper variants long-term.

> AGENT

Genuine business question — let me give you a real opinion, not CV-mode advice.

### The honest answer: yes, but it's two separate decisions

**Decision 1: For client/freelance work — should it run under Reliq?**

**Yes, almost certainly.** Reasons that are actually load-bearing:

1. **Invoicing through a company looks more professional** than invoices from a person, especially to enterprise / larger clients. Many corporates prefer (or require) contracting with a company, not a sole trader.
2. **Limited liability.** If you ever do work where a client could sue (web development that breaks something, AI consulting that produces bad output, etc.), a Ltd company shields your personal assets.
3. **UK tax efficiency.** At certain income levels, drawing income via a Ltd company (small salary + dividends) is materially more tax-efficient than self-employed sole trader, especially above ~£50k/year of freelance income.
4. **Portfolio continuity.** "Reliq has delivered for Blueprint Builders, MassPeople" reads stronger than "Sumeet did some stuff."
5. **Optionality for scaling.** If you ever want to bring on a collaborator / contractor / partner, the entity exists.
6. **Brand persistence.** Clients refer "Reliq" to other clients in a way they wouldn't refer "Sumeet's freelance services."

**Counter-arguments:**

1. **Overhead.** Ltd company = annual confirmation statements, corporation tax filings, accountant (~£800-1500/year), payroll if you draw salary. Worth it above ~£20k/year of freelance income; questionable below.
2. **Looks "fake" if obviously one-person.** Clients sometimes prefer the honesty of "I'm an individual contractor" over "we're a studio (also just one person)." Easy to mitigate — be honest about it on the site and in pitches.

**Net:** if you're going to do freelance/consulting work *at all*, run it through Reliq. Even if it's intermittent.

### Decision 2: For CV positioning — should you lead with Reliq?

**Different question.** The CV is about positioning for the *next role*. If the next role is:
- **Mercor / full-time engineering employment** → CV leads with individual track record. Reliq is a small entry.
- **Enterprise consulting clients / Reliq business development** → entirely different doc with Reliq leading.

You can do both at the same time. Many engineers run a Ltd company on the side for occasional consulting *and* hold full-time engineering jobs. The two don't conflict legally or strategically.

### What this means concretely

- **Run your freelance/consulting work through Reliq.** Take Blueprint Builders, take any future client work, invoice via Reliq Studios Ltd if it's incorporated (or incorporate it if not).
- **Keep Reliq small on your engineering CV.** One Experience entry, 1-2 bullets, doesn't lead. Mercor and engineering employers see you as an engineer first.
- **Build a separate one-pager / pitch deck for Reliq client outreach.** Different doc, different audience, different framing. Reliq leads there.

### The actual hard part

The thing that determines whether Reliq grows into a real business isn't the brand — it's whether you spend time on **client acquisition**. Brand without clients is decoration. If you're going to invest in Reliq, the leverage is in:
- Networking / referrals from existing clients
- A clear service offering (web dev? AI infra? both?)
- Pricing
- Marketing (the website is the easy part; outbound is the hard part)

That's a separate conversation from CV-drafting and a much bigger time commitment.

### Recommendation for *right now* (CV decision)

Going with **Option 1 from earlier**: small Reliq Studios entry on the master CV (Blueprint Builders as the named work, factual, no overclaiming). Mercor variant cuts it. You preserve all your options and lock in nothing. We can revisit when you decide to seriously push Reliq client work.

**Sound right? If yes, we start building.**

The platform contracts (DataAnnotation, Mercor) are between *Sumeet the individual* and them. But your **trading identity** for independent work can absolutely be Reliq — that's exactly what a trading-as / DBA name does for sole traders.

### Should you incorporate?

**Honest answer: probably not right now.** UK Ltd company starts paying back at roughly:

- **£30-40k+ annual freelance profit** — tax efficiency starts to outweigh the overhead.
- **Below that** — sole trader is simpler, cheaper, less admin.

- ~200hrs DataAnnotation YTD (call it £10-25k depending on rate)
- Blueprint Builders — one-off
- Elijah is equity, not cash

**Triggers to incorporate later:**
1. Freelance profit clearly exceeds £30-40k/year.
2. A specific client wants to engage a company (not an individual).
3. You commit to building Reliq as primary income.
4. You take on real liability risk (consulting work that could be sued over).

### But here's the issue for the CV

A portfolio tag works on legibility-of-theme. A CV bullet works on contractual reality. Some of those Reliq Labs tags can't survive a CV interview probe:

- **Mako Trading (market-data-handler)** — Mako was your **employer**, paid you a salary. You did NSE handler work as a Mako employee, not as Reliq Labs delivering services to Mako. Framing it as "Reliq Labs" on a CV would read as fabrication.
- **IBM (rogue-ap-detection, ibm-biodiversity)** — IBM Extreme Blue internship, IBM paid you. Not Reliq.
- **Bristol Airport** — KCL university group project. Definitely not Reliq.
- **Argus, Aether** — personal infrastructure. Could legitimately be "Reliq Labs internal tooling" since they support your Reliq operations, but they're not commercial engagements.

**Honestly Reliq on the CV:**
- ✅ **Blueprint Builders** — paid client of Reliq Studios.
- ✅ **AI training contracts** — your independent freelance work under Reliq trading name.
- ✅ **sumeetsaini.com, arcanecodex** — your own brand sites, fine to credit as Reliq Studios self-work.
- 🟡 **Elijah** — sweat-for-equity is personal; can plausibly say "engaged via Reliq Labs" but it's a stretch since you ARE the technical lead and equity is yours personally. Cleaner as standalone.
- ❌ **Mako, IBM, Bristol Airport** — paid by external orgs as employee/intern/student. Cannot be Reliq.

### CV (different conventions)

CVs follow employer-as-entry-header convention because that's the format hiring managers parse. So:

- **Mako Trading** = entry header. Not "Reliq Labs."
- **IBM** = entry header. Not "Reliq Labs."
- **King's College London** = entry header for the Research Assistant role.
- **Reliq Studios** = its own entry header, covering the work that *was* actually done under your sole-trader brand (Blueprint Builders + AI training contracts).
- **Elijah** = its own entry header (Stealth AI Startup, sweat-for-equity).

This isn't a statement about what's "yours" — every line on this CV is your work. It's about which document convention is being used. CVs use payer-as-header; portfolios use whatever-the-owner-wants.

Right — read the old CVs. Important date corrections noted (Reliq Sept 2025, Stealth AI April 2026). And you've raised three genuine questions. Honest take on each:

### 1. Date corrections

| Entry | Old | Corrected |
|-------|-----|-----------|
| Reliq Studios | 2024 | **Sept 2025 – Present** |
| Stealth AI Startup | Sept 2025 | **April 2026 – Present** |

Updating my mental model.

### 2. Do projects go on the CV?

**Yes, for you specifically.** You're 3 years YOE so still in the zone where projects materially help. And **Aether** + **Argus** are substantial — multi-service infrastructure, public on GitHub, demonstrate current AI agent work that's highly Mercor-relevant. They don't belong as Experience entries (no client, no employer), but they belong as a **small Projects section** below Experience.

Sizing: 2-3 line items, no more. Lead with Argus (most relevant for AI roles).

### 3. Skills section — yes, but at the bottom

Methodology §8: FAANG hiring managers want it at the top; UK CVs put it bottom; mixed strategy works fine. Modern reality is **ATS keyword matching matters** (~75% rejection rate). You need the keywords *somewhere* legible.

Recommend: small Skills section near the bottom, organized by category. Modular so we can reorder per variant.

```
Languages:  C++20, Python, JavaScript, Lua, Shell
AI / ML:    LiteLLM, vLLM, HuggingFace, TensorFlow, Prophet (research)
Infra:      Docker, Nginx, GitHub Actions, Cloudflare Zero Trust, PostgreSQL, AWS (S3/Lambda/DynamoDB), systemd
Web:        React, Hugo, Three.js, Flask
```

### 4. Soft skills — **demonstrated, not listed**

This is the one where I'll push back a little. Looking at the old CVs, the soft-skill *section* (the "Personal Skills" sidebar with things like "Swift Comprehension of Problems and Text", "Mentoring and Tutoring Peers") is the **single weakest part of those old CVs**. Industry consensus: unsupported soft-skill lists are pattern-skipped by recruiters because anyone can claim "excellent communication".

**But you're not wrong that soft skills are a real strength** — your CV is unusually communication-heavy. Mako stakeholder coordination, IBM weekly presentations to mixed audiences, KCL AI Soc president with 100+ members, IBM LabHack live demo on stage, private tutor / debate mentor history.

The honest way to surface these is to **demonstrate them in bullets**, not list them. Compare:

> ❌ Skills: "Excellent communicator", "Stakeholder management", "Leadership"

vs.

> ✅ "Coordinated directly with the exchange, broker, and internal data-pipeline and infrastructure teams" (Mako bullet — demonstrates cross-functional comms)
> ✅ "Presented weekly to technical and non-technical stakeholders at IBM Hursley" (IBM bullet — demonstrates audience-spanning comms)
> ✅ "President — designed and ran weekly AI labs for 100+ members" (KCL AI Soc — demonstrates leadership)

The Profile (line 1) can also explicitly position you: *"Engineer with a track record across AI platforms, low-latency systems, and bringing technical work to non-technical stakeholders."*

**That's how senior CVs surface soft skills.** Lists die; lived evidence survives.

# My Dotfiles

This repository contains my system configuration files, managed with GNU Stow. This approach addresses several common issues:
* Easy recovery from messed up configurations
* Quick experimentation without permanent installation
* Seamless system transitions
* Clean tracking and removal of software

## Setup

I use GNU [Stow](https://www.gnu.org/software/stow/) to manage dotfiles. To set up:
```bash
stow ~/dotfiles --dotfiles
```

While Nix Home Manager is an alternative, I find Stow simpler for managing a focused set of dotfiles.

## Configurations

### Window Manager
- **Aerospace** - Tiling window manager configuration (`dot-config/aerospace/`)

### Development Tools
- **Neovim** - Lua-based configuration with plugins, keybindings, and custom scripts (`dot-config/nvim/`)
- **Git** - Git configuration (`dot-config/git/`)
- **GitHub CLI** - gh configuration and hosts (`dot-config/gh/`)

### Terminal
- **Kitty** - Terminal emulator with themes, shortcuts, and quick access configs (`dot-config/kitty/`)
- **Starship** - Custom prompt configuration (`dot-config/starship/`)
- **ZSH** - Modular shell configuration with aliases, functions, and plugins (`dot-config/zsh/`)
- **Tmux** - Terminal multiplexer with status bar and keybindings (`dot-config/tmux/`)

### Productivity
- **Taskwarrior** - Task management with custom themes and hooks (`dot-config/task/`)
- **Timewarrior** - Time tracking configuration (`dot-config/timewarrior/`)
- **Atuin** - Shell history management (`dot-config/atuin/`)

### Utilities
- **Fastfetch** - System information tool configuration (`dot-config/fastfetch/`)
- **Karabiner-Elements** - Keyboard customization (`dot-config/karabiner/`)
- **Hammerspoon** - macOS automation framework (`dot-config/hammerspoon/`)
- **Raycast** - Launcher extensions (`dot-config/raycast/`)
- **Yazi** - File manager configuration (`dot-config/yazi/`)

### Applications
- **Obsidian** - Note-taking app configuration (`codex/dot-obsidian/`)
- **Sioyek** - PDF viewer preferences (`dot-config/sioyek/`)
- **Spotify Player** - CLI client configuration (`dot-config/spotify-player/`)
- **Stats** - macOS system monitor config (`stats/`)
- **Brave** - Browser bookmarks and extensions (`Library/Application Support/BraveSoftware/`)

### Graphics
- **Inkscape** - Vector graphics editor preferences (`dot-config/inkscape/`)

### Nix
- **Nix** - Declarative package management with flake configuration (`dot-config/nix/`)

### Miscellaneous
- **npm** - Node.js package manager configuration (`dot-config/npm/`)
- **Wallpapers** - Custom wallpaper collection (`wallpapers/`)
